comment.original_text:
PETER CHARDON BROOKS, the other grandfather, died January 1, 1849, bequeathing what was supposed to be the largest estate in Boston, about two million dollars, to his seven surviving children. Among them were three daughters--Charlotte, married to Edward Everett; Ann, married to Nathaniel Frothingham, minister of the First Church; and Abigail Brown, married September 3, 1829, to Charles Francis Adams. Their first child, born in 1830, was a daughter, named Louisa Catherine, after her Johnson grandmother; the second was a son, named John Quincy, after his President grandfather; the third took his father's name, Charles Francis; while the fourth, being of less account, was in a way given to his mother, who named him Henry Brooks, after a favorite brother just lost.

One might have sought long in much larger and older societies for three brothers-in-law more distinguished or more scholarly than Edward Everett, Dr. Frothingham, and Mr. Adams. One might have sought equally long for seven brothers-in-law more unlike. Mr. Everett, one of the most ambitious of Bostonians, had broken bounds early in life by leaving the Unitarian pulpit to take a seat in Congress, and had risen to undisputed rank second only to Daniel Webster as the orator and representative figure of Boston. Dr. Frothingham belonged to the same clerical school. Neither of them had much in common with Mr. Adams, who was a younger man, greatly biassed by his father, and by the inherited feud between Quincy and State Street; but personal relations were friendly as far as a boy could see, and the innumerable cousins went regularly to the First Church every Sunday in winter, and slept through their uncle's sermons. For two hundred years the First Church had seen the same little boys, sleeping more or less soundly under the same or similar conditions, and dimly conscious of the same feuds; but the feuds had never ceased, and the boys had always grown up to inherit them.

By 1850 the quarrels of John Adams and John Quincy Adams were no longer acutely personal; the game was considered as drawn; and Charles Francis Adams might then have taken his inherited rights of political leadership in succession to Mr. Webster and Mr. Everett, his seniors. Instead, he drew himself aloof and renewed the old war which had already lasted since 1700. He could not help it. With the record of J. Q. Adams fresh in the popular memory, his son and his only representative could not make terms with the slave-power, and the slave-power overshadowed all the great Boston interests. No doubt Mr. Adams had principles of his own, as well as inherited, but even his children, who as yet had no principles, could equally little follow the lead of Mr. Webster or even of Mr. Seward. They were anti-slavery by birth, as their name was Adams and their home was Quincy. Had State Street been Paradise, they must hunger for it in vain, and it hardly needed Daniel Webster to act as archangel with the flaming sword, to order them away from the door.

Time and experience, which alter all perspectives, altered this among the rest, and taught the boy gentler judgment, but even when only ten years old, his face was already fixed, and his heart was stone, against State Street; his education was warped beyond recovery in the direction of Puritan politics. The year 1848 was like enough to the year 1776 to make a fair parallel. The parallel was complete when, a few months after the death of John Quincy Adams, a convention of anti-slavery delegates met at Buffalo to organize a new party and named candidates for the general election in November: for President, Martin Van Buren; for Vice-President, Charles Francis Adams.

The stamp of 1848 was almost as indelible as the stamp of 1776, but in the eighteenth or any earlier century, the stamp mattered less because it was standard, and every one bore it; while men whose lives were to fall in the generation between 1865 and 1900 had, first of all, to get rid of it, and take the stamp that belonged to their time. This was their education. To outsiders, immigrants, adventurers, it was easy, but the old Puritan nature rebelled against change. The Puritan thought his thought higher and his moral standards better than those of his successors. So they were. Nature had given to the boy Henry a character that, in any previous century, would have led him into the Church; he inherited dogma and a priori thought from the beginning of time; and he scarcely needed a violent reaction like anti-slavery politics to sweep him back into Puritanism with a violence as great as that of a religious war.

Thus far he had nothing to do with it; his education was chiefly inheritance, and during the next five or six years, his father alone counted for much. If he were to worry successfully through life's quicksands, he must depend chiefly on his father's pilotage; but, for his father, the channel lay clear, while for himself an unknown ocean lay beyond. The generation that lived from 1840 to 1870 could do very well with the old forms of education; that which had its work to do between 1870 and 1900 needed something quite new.

His father's character was therefore the larger part of his education, as far as any single person affected it, and the son was always a much interested critic of his father's mind and temper. To his son Henry, the quality that distinguished his father from all the other figures in the family group, was that, in his opinion, Charles Francis Adams possessed the only perfectly balanced mind that ever existed in the name. For a hundred years, every newspaper scribbler had derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment. Charles Francis Adams was singular for mental poise--absence of self-assertion or self-consciousness--the faculty of standing apart without seeming aware that he was alone--a balance of mind and temper that neither challenged nor avoided notice, nor admitted question of superiority or inferiority, of jealousy, of personal motives, from any source, even under great pressure. This unusual poise became the more striking to his son Henry as he learned to measure the mental faculties themselves, which were in no way exceptional either for depth or range. Charles Francis Adams's memory was hardly above the average; his mind was not bold like his grandfather's or restless like his father's, or imaginative or oratorical--still less mathematical; but it worked with singular perfection, admirable self-restraint, and instinctive mastery of form. Within its range it was a model. He stood alone. He had no master--hardly even his father. He had no scholars--hardly even his sons.

Almost alone among his Boston contemporaries, he was not English in feeling or in sympathies, and in his case this went further and became indifference to social distinction. Never once in forty years of intimacy did his son notice in him a trace of snobbishness. Never did his son see him flatter or vilify, or show a sign of envy or jealousy; never a shade of vanity or self-conceit. Never a tone of arrogance! Never a gesture of pride!

No one ever charged Charles Francis Adams with want of judgment. The critics charged him with just the opposite defect. They called him cold. No doubt, such perfect poise--such intuitive self-adjustment--was not maintained by nature without a sacrifice of the qualities which would have upset it. No doubt, too, that even his restless-minded, introspective, self-conscious children who knew him best were much too ignorant of the world and of human nature to suspect how rare and complete was the model before their eyes. The world never loved perfect poise. What the world does love is commonly absence of poise, for it has to be amused. Had Mr. Adams's nature been cold, he would have followed Mr. Webster, Mr. Everett, Mr. Seward, and Mr. Winthrop in the lines of party discipline and self-interest. Had it been less balanced than it was, he would have gone with Mr. Garrison, Mr. Wendell Phillips, Mr. Edmund Quincy, and Theodore Parker, into secession. Between the two paths he found an intermediate one, distinctive and characteristic--he set up a party of his own.

The group of men with whom Mr. Adams associated himself, and whose social centre was the house in Mount Vernon Street, numbered only three: Dr. John G. Palfrey, Richard H. Dana, and Charles Sumner. Dr. Palfrey was the oldest, and in spite of his clerical education, was to a boy often the most agreeable, for his talk was lighter and his range wider than that of the others. Born to be a man of the world, he forced himself to be clergyman, professor, or statesman. Dana affected to be still before the mast, and only as one got to know him better one found the man of rather excessive refinement trying with success to work like a day-laborer, deliberately hardening his skin to the burden, as though he were still carrying hides at Monterey. He, too, talked well, and his mind worked close to its subject, as a lawyer's should; but disguise and silence it as he liked, it was aristocratic to the tenth generation.

In that respect, and in that only, Charles Sumner was like him, but Sumner, in almost every other quality, was quite different from his three associates--altogether out of line. He adored English standards, and Boston admired him chiefly for his social success in England and on the Continent. Sumner was socially ostracized, and so were all the other avowed anti-slavery leaders, but for them it mattered less, because they had houses and families of their own; while Sumner had neither wife nor household, and, though the most socially ambitious of all, he could enter hardly half-a-dozen houses in Boston. Few days passed when he did not pass some time in Mount Vernon Street. Even with that, his solitude was glacial, and reacted on his character.

The boy Henry worshipped him, and if he ever regarded any older man as a personal friend, it was Mr. Sumner. The relation of Mr. Sumner in the household was far closer than any relation of blood. None of the uncles approached such intimacy. Sumner was the boy's ideal of greatness; the highest product of nature and art. To the twelve-year-old boy, his father, Dr. Palfrey, Mr. Dana, were men, more or less like what he himself might become; but Mr. Sumner was a different order--heroic.

As the boy grew up to be ten or twelve years old, his father gave him a writing-table in one of the alcoves of his Boston library, and there, winter after winter, Henry worked over his Latin Grammar and listened to these four gentlemen discussing the course of anti-slavery politics. The discussions were always serious, and habitual because Mr. Adams had undertaken to edit a newspaper as the organ of these gentlemen. At the same time Mr. Adams was editing the "Works" of his grandfather John Adams, and made the boy read texts for proof-correction. In after years his father sometimes complained that Henry had shown very little consciousness of punctuation; but the boy regarded this part of school life only as a warning, if he ever grew up to write dull discussions in the newspapers, to try to be dull in some different way from that of his great-grandfather. The boy got as little education, fitting him for his own time, from the one as from the other, and he got no more from his contact with the gentlemen themselves who were all types of the past.

Down to 1850, and even later, New England society was still directed by the professions. In politics it was the old Ciceronian idea of government by the best that produced the long line of New England statesmen. Thus Boston chose Daniel Webster, and Edward Everett held the rank in regular succession to Webster.

The boy naturally took for granted that this sort of world was the world which he was to fit. Had he known Europe he would have learned no better. The Paris of Louis Philippe, Guizot, and de Tocqueville, as well as the London of Robert Peel, Macaulay, and John Stuart Mill, were but varieties of the same upper-class bourgeoisie that felt instinctive cousinship with the Boston of Ticknor, Prescott, and Motley. England's middle-class government was the ideal of human progress.

Even the violent reaction after 1848 never for a moment shook the true faith. No one, except Karl Marx, foresaw radical change. What announced it? The world was producing sixty or seventy million tons of coal, and might be using nearly a million steam-horsepower, just beginning to make itself felt. All experience since the creation of man, all divine revelation or human science, conspired to deceive and betray a twelve-year-old boy who took for granted that his ideas, which were alone respectable, would be alone respected.

Viewed from Mount Vernon Street, the problem of life was as simple as it was classic. Social perfection was sure, because human nature worked for Good, and three instruments were all she asked--Suffrage, Common Schools, and Press. On these points doubt was forbidden. Education was divine, and man needed only a correct knowledge of facts to reach perfection. Nothing quieted doubt so completely as the mental calm of the Unitarian clergy, who controlled society and Harvard College. For them, difficulties might be ignored; doubts were waste of thought; nothing exacted solution. Boston had solved the universe; or had offered and realized the best solution yet tried. The problem was worked out.

Of all the conditions of his youth which afterwards puzzled the grown-up man, this disappearance of religion puzzled him most. The boy went to church twice every Sunday; he prayed; he went through all the forms; but neither to him nor to his brothers or sisters was religion real. Even the mild discipline of the Unitarian Church was so irksome that they all threw it off at the first possible moment, and never afterwards entered a church. The religious instinct had vanished, and could not be revived, although one made in later life many efforts to recover it. That the most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual, should disappear, might be a personal defect of his own; but that the most intelligent society, led by the most intelligent clergy, should have persuaded itself that all the problems which had convulsed human thought from earliest recorded time, were not worth discussing, seemed to him the most curious social phenomenon he had to account for in a long life. The faculty of turning away one's eyes as one approaches a chasm is not unusual, and Boston showed, under the lead of Mr. Webster, how successfully it could be done in politics; but in politics a certain number of men did at least protest. In religion and philosophy no one protested. Such protest as was made took forms more simple than the silence, like the deism of Theodore Parker. The less aggressive protest of Ralph Waldo Emerson, was, from an old-world point of view, less serious. It was naif.

The children reached manhood without knowing religion, and their education became, almost of necessity, the more literary and political. From childhood the boys were accustomed to hear, almost every day, table-talk as good as they were ever likely to hear again. The eldest child, Louisa, was one of the most sparkling creatures her brother met in a long and varied experience of bright women. The oldest son, John, was afterwards regarded as one of the best talkers in Boston society. Mr. Adams, who talked relatively little, was always a good listener, and laughed over a witticism till he choked.

Mr. Adams read much aloud, especially political literature when it was satirical, like the "Epistles" of "Hosea Biglow," with great delight to the youth. The boy Henry drifted into the mental indolence of history, and read shelves of eighteenth-century poetry, but when his father offered his own set of Wordsworth as a gift on condition of reading it through, he declined. The boy was thirty years old before his education reached Wordsworth.

His father made no effort to force his mind, but left him free play, and this was perhaps best; only he tried to teach him French. The boy had a large and overpowering set of brothers and sisters, who were modes or replicas of the same type. They knew no more than he what they wanted or what to do for it, but all were conscious that they would like to control power in some form. They amounted to one individual with half-a-dozen sides or facets. What no one knew was whether the individual who thought himself a representative of this type, was fit to deal with life.

If school helped, it was only by reaction. The dislike of school was so strong as to be a positive gain. His memory was slow, and the effort painful. He thought his mind a good enough machine, if it were given time to act, but it acted wrong if hurried. Schoolmasters never gave time.

He always reckoned his school-days, from ten to sixteen years old, as time thrown away. For success in the life imposed on him he needed, as afterwards appeared, the facile use of only four tools: Mathematics, French, German, and Spanish. These four tools were necessary to his success in life, but he never controlled any one of them.

Boston at that time offered few healthy resources for boys or men, and no sport worth learning. From none of its amusements could the boy learn anything likely to be of use to him in the world. As far as happiness went, the happiest hours of the boy's education were passed in summer lying on a musty heap of Congressional Documents in the old farmhouse at Quincy, reading "Quentin Durward," "Ivanhoe," and "The Talisman," and raiding the garden at intervals for peaches and pears. On the whole he learned most then.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's sentence beginning 'He could not be convinced that moral standards had nothing to do with it...'
findings.plan_relation: Required. The essentials name 'So they were' as part of the Puritan-bias argument.
findings.reader_effect: Adams's turn is that the Puritan was right about morals and wrong that morals mattered. Without it, the line reads as unqualified agreement, and the reason for the old nature's resistance to change goes with it.
findings.title: 'So they were' loses its dry reversal

findings.claim: The revision reduces the section to the Webster–Everett succession. It drops 'each profession were a church,' 'Sumner aspired to break the succession, but not the system,' and the Mount Vernon group as 'statesmen, not politicians.' The first draft had kept all three.
findings.counterevidence: 'This sort of world' in paragraph 15 still resolves to the professional system, and chapter 005 remains readable on its own.

evidence.quote: The little group of men in Mount Vernon Street were an offshoot of this system; they were statesmen, not politicians

With this bargain Mr. Adams and his statesman friends would have nothing to do

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'Charles Sumner aspired to break the succession, but not the system' and the first draft's 'statesmen, not politicians' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: Required. The essentials list 'government... by the best' and the Webster succession. The cross-chapter link is a planning omission.
findings.reader_effect: The section no longer explains the boy's own world, only Webster's. Chapter 005's revision relies on 'his statesman friends' recoiling from machine politics, a contrast this chapter no longer sets up.
findings.title: Mount Vernon circle cut loose from 'government by the best'

findings.claim: In the source, 'the one... the other' refers to the Boston Whig debates and John Adams's controversies. The first draft cut the Boston Whig sentence, and the revision keeps the residue unchanged.
findings.counterevidence: The two editing projects mentioned earlier in the paragraph can serve loosely as the pair.

evidence.quote: Yet the discussions in the Boston Whig were carried on in much the same style as those of John Adams and his opponent

findings.plan_relation: An authorized compression that leaves a dangling residue.
findings.reader_effect: The reader has to guess what is being paired. The joke's sting is also lost: the newspaper the boy hears debated is as dull as his great-grandfather's prose.
findings.title: 'From the one as from the other' has lost its pair

findings.claim: The revision cuts the sentence saying the political party 'became a chief influence in the education of the boy Henry in the six years 1848 to 1854' and shaped his plastic character. Paragraph 10 now opens straight on the group of men.
findings.counterevidence: 'Set up a party of his own' immediately precedes the paragraph, so the link remains inferable.

evidence.quote: This political party became a chief influence in the education of the boy Henry in the six years 1848 to 1854
violently affected his character at the moment when character is plastic
The group of men with whom Mr. Adams associated himself, and whose social centre was the house in Mount Vernon Street

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's opening sentence of paragraph 11.
findings.plan_relation: A planning omission. Not listed as optional, and it carries the chapter's time frame.
findings.reader_effect: The causal hinge between the father's middle path and the Mount Vernon circle disappears. So does the only anchor for the chapter's 1848–1854 span.
findings.title: Paragraph linking 'party of his own' to the boy's formation dropped

findings.claim: The revision cuts the clause that the sons would pay for the pilotage 'with their lives wasted on battle-fields or in misdirected energies.' The first draft kept it.
findings.counterevidence: The essential contrast between the father's channel and the sons' ocean, and between the two generations, is intact.

evidence.quote: it mattered little to his success whether they paid it with their lives wasted on battle-fields or in misdirected energies and lost opportunity
The task done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage
while for himself an unknown ocean lay beyond. The generation that lived from 1840 to 1870

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's two sentences beginning 'His father's business in life...'
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff. The essential core is kept.
findings.reader_effect: The metaphor keeps its clear channel and unknown ocean but loses its dark edge and the shadow of the coming war.
findings.title: Pilotage loses its bitter cost clause

findings.claim: The first draft cut 'the boy had nothing to complain of' and the following 'never complained' lines. The revision then dropped the rote-learning reason ('compelled to learn by memory'), so 'His memory was slow' arrives without context. It also dropped the stated payoff of the four tools ('With these, he could master...').
findings.counterevidence: V7 and V8 are verbatim, and 'positive gain' and 'time thrown away' convey the core.

evidence.quote: He hated it because he was here with a crowd of other boys and compelled to learn by memory a quantity of things that did not amuse him.
With these, he could master in very short time any special branch of inquiry, and feel at home in any society.
The dislike of school was so strong as to be a positive gain. His memory was slow, and the effort painful.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'compelled to learn by memory' sentence and the 'With these, he could master...' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff. The essentials are kept.
findings.reader_effect: Hatred of school reads as a grievance against a bad school rather than against method, and the tools list loses its rationale.
findings.title: School grievance and tools passage thinned

remaining_concerns: The two necessary repairs add about 73 words, against a target of about +19, leaving the chapter roughly 50 words (≈1.8%) over 3000. No remaining material is listed as optional, and further cuts would hit essentials or protected passages, so the overage is accepted rather than sacrificing meaning.
Restoring 'Sumner aspired to break the succession, but not the system' and 'statesmen, not politicians' (F3) would strengthen the setup for chapter 005, if a later pass finds room.

replacements.new: which would have upset it. No doubt, too, that even his restless-minded, introspective, self-conscious children who knew him best were much too ignorant of the world and of human nature to suspect how rare and complete was the model before their eyes. A coarser instrument would have impressed them more. The world never loved perfect poise.
replacements.old: which would have upset it. The world never loved perfect poise.
replacements.reason: Restores the source's second 'No doubt' hedge and the transition into V3, per the plan's stated risk.

replacements.new: So they were. He could not be convinced that moral standards had nothing to do with it, and that utilitarian morality was good enough for him, as it was for the graceless. Nature had given
replacements.old: So they were. Nature had given
replacements.reason: Restores the source's dry reversal after 'So they were.'

evidence.quote: derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment.
The critics charged him with just the opposite defect from his father's restlessness.

adjudications.reason: The draft keeps V2, the hedges and V3, but cuts the scribblers' paradox. That paradox frames the father's poise as a public liability, which is the essential's 'called cold' irony and the plan's stated over-compression risk. It also leaves the 'opposite defect' propped up by an inserted phrase ('from his father's restlessness') that is not in the source. Restoring the two source sentences lets the source's plain 'opposite defect' stand. The Napoleons sentence is an optional illustration, and V3 already carries that point.

evidence.quote: for his father, the channel lay clear, while for himself an unknown ocean lay beyond

adjudications.reason: The pilotage essential is the clear channel versus the unknown ocean, plus the 1840–1870 versus 1870–1900 generations. Both survive intact. The 'sons pay for the pilotage' reversal is a legitimate tradeoff under a tight budget.

evidence.quote: Dana's ideal of life was to be a great Englishman
He, too, adored English standards

adjudications.reason: 'He, too, adored English standards' refers back to the Anglophilia of Palfrey and Dana. Both instances were cut, so the draft never establishes it. Deleting 'too' is the smallest repair, and Sumner's Anglophilia stays.

evidence.quote: to write dull discussions in the newspapers, to try to be dull in some different way from that of his great-grandfather

adjudications.reason: The sentence just before supplies the pair: dull newspaper discussions versus those of his great-grandfather. 'From the one as from the other' therefore still parses, and 'all types of the past' keeps the essential.

evidence.quote: For them, difficulties might be ignored; doubts were waste of thought; nothing exacted solution.

adjudications.reason: Unitarian calm survives in the draft through 'mental calm of the Unitarian clergy', 'doubts were waste of thought' and V6. The vanished-religion puzzle remains fully set up. The 'no doctrine' sentence is useful but not necessary.

evidence.quote: he set up a party of his own.

adjudications.reason: The plan does not require this sentence. The move from 'a party of his own' to the Mount Vernon Street group reads cleanly, and V1 already marks the political warp of his education.

findings.claim: The first draft kept the paradox that scribblers abused the older Adamses for want of judgment and Charles Francis for his judgment. The revision cuts it, so 'The critics charged him' now arrives without its attributed setup. The Napoleons illustration of the world's love of imbalance is also gone.
findings.counterevidence: 'restless like his father's' in paragraph 7 lets 'opposite defect' still parse, and the 'No doubt' hedges and V3 survive.

evidence.quote: derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment.
every newspaper scribbler had derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment.
The critics charged him with just the opposite defect from his father's restlessness. They called him cold.
Napoleons and Andrew Jacksons amuse it, but it is not amused by perfect balance.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the two scribbler sentences after V2.
findings.plan_relation: Required. This is the father's-poise essential and its stated risk.
findings.reader_effect: This loses the central ironic symmetry that frames the father's poise as a liability with the public, which is exactly the over-compression risk the plan flags.
findings.title: Newspaper judgment paradox cut; 'The critics' left unintroduced

findings.claim: The revision drops the father's task of fixing the slave-power's bounds, and the dry reversal that his sons would pay for the pilotage with lives wasted on battle-fields or misdirected energies.
findings.counterevidence: The clear-channel versus unknown-ocean contrast and the 1840–1870 versus 1870–1900 generational claim remain.

evidence.quote: The task done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage; and it mattered little to his success whether they paid it with their lives wasted on battle-fields
The task done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage
while for himself an unknown ocean lay beyond. The generation that lived from 1840 to 1870 could do very well with the old forms of education

findings.minimal_repair: Reinsert 'The task done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage...' (one sentence).
findings.plan_relation: Required. This is the pilotage essential.
findings.reader_effect: The pilotage image shrinks to a contrast between the father's clear channel and the sons' unknown ocean, losing its edge of cost and the old man's irony.
findings.title: Sons paying for the pilotage is cut

findings.claim: In the source, 'too' refers back to Palfrey's Pall Mall yearning and Dana's ideal of being a great Englishman. Both were cut, so 'too' implies an Anglophilia the draft never shows.
findings.counterevidence: The phrase 'aristocratic to the tenth generation' loosely suggests the same taste.

evidence.quote: Dana's ideal of life was to be a great Englishman, with a seat on the front benches of the House of Commons
He, too, adored English standards, and Boston admired him chiefly for his social success in England and on the Continent.
He, too, adored English standards, and Boston admired him chiefly for his social success in England and on the Continent.

findings.minimal_repair: Keep 'Dana's ideal of life was to be a great Englishman' without the woolsack clause, or delete 'too'.
findings.plan_relation: Planning omission. Grouping 'woolsack' with the Evarts quotation as an optional cut removed the only Anglophile antecedent.
findings.reader_effect: Readers are told that Sumner shares an English bent with his associates that the abridgment never established.
findings.title: 'He, too, adored English standards' lacks an antecedent

findings.claim: The source sets the Boston Whig discussions in the same style as John Adams's controversies, then concludes 'from the one as from the other.' With the parallel cut, the pair must be inferred from scattered mentions of the newspaper and the Works.
findings.counterevidence: The newspaper and the Works are both named earlier in the same paragraph.

evidence.quote: Yet the discussions in the Boston Whig were carried on in much the same style as those of John Adams and his opponent
The boy got as little education, fitting him for his own time, from the one as from the other
The boy got as little education, fitting him for his own time, from the one as from the other

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the Boston Whig parallel sentence.
findings.plan_relation: Required. This is part of the library-alcove essential: 'Everything he absorbed was of the past.'
findings.reader_effect: The point that 1850 political prose was 1770s prose, and so equally useless for his own time, blurs.
findings.title: 'From the one as from the other' has lost its parallel

findings.claim: The revision drops 'Politics offered no difficulties... moral law was a sure guide' and changes 'also sure' to 'sure'. It also removes the clergy's boast that they insisted on no doctrine, only virtuous living.
findings.counterevidence: 'doubts were waste of thought' and V6 still convey complacency.

evidence.quote: They proclaimed as their merit that they insisted on no doctrine, but taught, or tried to teach, the means of leading a virtuous, useful, unselfish life
They proclaimed as their merit that they insisted on no doctrine
Social perfection was sure, because human nature worked for Good, and three instruments were all she asked

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'insisted on no doctrine' sentence and the moral-law clause.
findings.plan_relation: Required. This is the Unitarian calm essential.
findings.reader_effect: The vanished-religion puzzle loses its key premise: a creedless church made doubt seem needless. The parallel that politics and society were both 'sure' is also lost.
findings.title: Unitarian 'no doctrine' premise and the moral-law clause are cut

findings.claim: The revision cuts the sentence saying the father's party was a chief influence on Henry from 1848 to 1854 and violently shaped his character. The chapter then jumps from 'a party of his own' straight to the guest list.
findings.counterevidence: V1's 'warped beyond recovery in the direction of Puritan politics' carries some of the same idea.

evidence.quote: This political party became a chief influence in the education of the boy Henry in the six years 1848 to 1854, and violently affected his character
This political party became a chief influence in the education of the boy Henry in the six years 1848 to 1854
The group of men with whom Mr. Adams associated himself, and whose social centre was the house in Mount Vernon Street, numbered only three

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the sentence at the head of paragraph 10.
findings.plan_relation: This sentence links the poise section to the circle section. The plan does not name it.
findings.reader_effect: This loses the explicit causal link between the father's politics and the boy's education, along with the chapter's date span.
findings.title: The party's formative effect on the boy is dropped

findings.claim: Both drafts drop the paradox 'almost a method in itself.' The revision also cuts why he hated school, which was rote memory, and the value of the four tools for mastering any branch and any society.
findings.counterevidence: V7, V8, 'positive gain', and 'from ten to sixteen' all remain.

evidence.quote: compelled to learn by memory a quantity of things that did not amuse him
With these, he could master in very short time any special branch of inquiry, and feel at home in any society.
With these, he could master in very short time any special branch of inquiry, and feel at home in any society.
The dislike of school was so strong as to be a positive gain. His memory was slow, and the effort painful.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'With these...' sentence, and optionally the memorization clause.
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff within the school essential.
findings.reader_effect: 'His memory was slow' now arrives abruptly. The four tools read as a bare list rather than a measure of capacity.
findings.title: School passage loses its paradox and the four tools lose their rationale

findings.claim: The first draft kept the Adamses' non-affinity with the pulpit and with the Websterian literati before 'He stood alone.' The revision appends the line to the faculties paragraph instead.
findings.counterevidence: The essential trio of lines survives verbatim, and the placement still reads sensibly.

evidence.quote: but Mr. Adams was not one of them; as a rule they were much too Websterian.
but the Adamses had little or no affinity with the pulpit.
Within its range it was a model. He stood alone. He had no master--hardly even his father.

findings.minimal_repair: Prefix 'Mr. Adams had no affinity with the pulpit, and the literary group were much too Websterian.'
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff. The plan keeps only 'stood alone / no master / no scholars'.
findings.reader_effect: His isolation from Boston's clergy and letters becomes generic independence, and an early cue for the later religion and Websterian-Boston themes is lost.
findings.title: 'He stood alone' loses its Boston cultural context

remaining_concerns: The estimated net change is about -53 words against the -55 target. I did not cut further to avoid trimming the father's-poise lists or the 'No doubt' qualifications.

replacements.new: Charles Francis Adams possessed the only perfectly balanced mind that ever existed in the name. For a hundred years, every newspaper scribbler had derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment. Charles Francis Adams was singular
replacements.old: Charles Francis Adams possessed the only perfectly balanced mind that ever existed in the name. Charles Francis Adams was singular

replacements.new: The critics charged him with just the opposite defect.
replacements.old: The critics charged him with just the opposite defect from his father's restlessness.
replacements.reason: With the paradox restored, return to the source wording and drop the inserted gloss.

replacements.old: So they were. He could not be convinced that moral standards had nothing to do with it, and that utilitarian morality was good enough for him, as it was for the graceless.
replacements.reason: Optional elaboration cut for length. 'So they were' and the Puritan bias remain.

replacements.new: model before their eyes.
replacements.old: model before their eyes. A coarser instrument would have impressed them more.
replacements.reason: Optional sentence. The hedges and V3 carry the point.

replacements.new: reacted on his character.
replacements.old: reacted on his character. His superiority was, indeed, real and incontestable; he was the classical ornament of the anti-slavery party.
replacements.reason: Optional cut. The hero-worship is fully carried by paragraph 12 and V4.

evidence.quote: No one ever charged Charles Francis Adams with this fault. The critics charged him with just the opposite defect.
Never a tone of arrogance! Never a gesture of pride!
The critics charged him with just the opposite defect. They called him cold.

adjudications.reason: In the revision, 'just the opposite defect' comes straight after a list of absent vices such as snobbery, flattery and arrogance. 'Cold' cannot sensibly be the opposite of any of those. The intended contrast, 'want of judgment', appears only two paragraphs earlier, in paragraph 7, and the source makes it explicit just before the critics' charge. A short clause using the source's own words restores the antecedent. The 'called cold, yet chose a middle path' argument then rests on its proper premise.

findings.claim: In the source, the critics' charge is opposite to J. Q. Adams's 'want of judgment.' The first draft cut that sentence but patched the reference as 'from his father's restlessness.' The revision removes the patch, so the sentence directly follows a list of absent vices.
findings.counterevidence: Paragraph 7 mentions the older Adamses' 'want of judgment,' but it is two paragraphs earlier.

evidence.quote: accompanied by mental restlessness and often by lamentable want of judgment. No one ever charged Charles Francis Adams with this fault. The critics charged him with just the opposite defect.
The critics charged him with just the opposite defect from his father's restlessness.
Never a tone of arrogance! Never a gesture of pride!
The critics charged him with just the opposite defect. They called him cold.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'No one ever charged Charles Francis Adams with this fault' preceded by a short JQA clause, or write 'just the opposite defect from the older Adamses' want of judgment.'
findings.plan_relation: Required: the plan's poise essentials include 'called cold, yet chose a middle path.'
findings.reader_effect: Readers cannot tell what 'cold' is the opposite of. The paragraph's argument (cold versus unbalanced, with Adams finding a middle path) starts from a broken premise.
findings.title: 'Just the opposite defect' has no antecedent

findings.claim: The sentence explaining the Puritan's error was cut. It says he could not see that moral standards had nothing to do with it. Without it, the concession now reads as unqualified endorsement.
findings.counterevidence: 'The old Puritan nature rebelled against change' still frames the passage as resistance.

evidence.quote: So they were. He could not be convinced that moral standards had nothing to do with it, and that utilitarian morality was good enough for him, as it was for the graceless.
So they were. He could not be convinced that moral standards had nothing to do with it
So they were. Nature had given to the boy Henry a character that, in any previous century, would have led him into the Church

findings.plan_relation: Required: the plan lists 'So they were' as an essential, and the voice profile calls for dry reversals.
findings.reader_effect: This flattens the dry reversal at the heart of Adams's argument about why the Puritan nature resisted the new stamp.
findings.title: 'So they were' loses its ironic reversal

findings.claim: Three passages were cut: the professions-as-churches line, Sumner breaking 'the succession, but not the system,' and the circle as 'statesmen, not politicians.' The section now ends on Everett, so 'this sort of world' no longer includes Henry's own household milieu.
findings.counterevidence: The Ciceronian 'government by the best' line and the European parallel survive.

evidence.quote: The little group of men in Mount Vernon Street were an offshoot of this system; they were statesmen, not politicians; they guided public opinion, but were little guided by it.
Charles Sumner aspired to break the succession, but not the system. The little group of men in Mount Vernon Street were statesmen, not politicians
Thus Boston chose Daniel Webster, and Edward Everett held the rank in regular succession to Webster.
The boy naturally took for granted that this sort of world was the world which he was to fit.
With this bargain Mr. Adams and his statesman friends would have nothing to do

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's two sentences: 'Charles Sumner aspired...' and 'The little group of men in Mount Vernon Street were statesmen...'
findings.plan_relation: Required: the plan lists 'New England government by the professions and by the best, the Webster succession.'
findings.reader_effect: This weakens the argument that the boy absorbed a system through his father's circle. It also thins the ground for 005's 'statesman friends' and the coalition lesson.
findings.title: Mount Vernon circle is disconnected from 'government by the best'

findings.claim: The revision cuts 'His superiority was, indeed, real and incontestable; he was the classical ornament of the anti-slavery party.' Sumner's portrait now ends on glacial solitude reacting on his character, and 'The boy Henry worshipped him' follows directly.
findings.counterevidence: Paragraph 12, with 'ideal of greatness' and 'heroic,' survives fully.

evidence.quote: His superiority was, indeed, real and incontestable; he was the classical ornament of the anti-slavery party
His superiority was, indeed, real and incontestable; he was the classical ornament of the anti-slavery party.
Even with that, his solitude was glacial, and reacted on his character.
The boy Henry worshipped him, and if he ever regarded any older man as a personal friend, it was Mr. Sumner.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 17-word superiority sentence after 'reacted on his character.'
findings.plan_relation: Required: dependency 1 asks for a strong bond, and the plan lists 'worshipped Sumner as heroic.'
findings.reader_effect: The hero-worship loses its stated basis. Ending on a character flaw slightly undercuts the 'heroic' idol the plan wants kept intact.
findings.title: Sumner's real superiority is dropped before the worship

findings.claim: Two sentences were cut. One explained that school compelled rote memorization; without it, 'His memory was slow' no longer explains the hatred. The other, 'With these, he could master... any special branch,' gave the four tools their reason. The 'almost a method in itself' paradox was also cut.
findings.counterevidence: V7, V8, 'positive gain,' and 'ten to sixteen' all survive.

evidence.quote: He hated it because he was here with a crowd of other boys and compelled to learn by memory a quantity of things that did not amuse him.
With these, he could master in very short time any special branch of inquiry, and feel at home in any society.
The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself.
The dislike of school was so strong as to be a positive gain. His memory was slow, and the effort painful.
Mathematics, French, German, and Spanish. These four tools were necessary to his success in life

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'compelled to learn by memory' sentence and the 'With these, he could master...' sentence.

findings.reader_effect: The mind-as-machine grievance (V7) and the four-tools measure arrive with weaker causal footing.

findings.claim: The revision drops the sons paying 'for the pilotage' with lives wasted on battle-fields or lost opportunity. It also drops 1848 as decisive, with 'never a side-path of escape.'
findings.counterevidence: The clear channel versus unknown ocean and both generation lines survive, which satisfies the plan's minimum.

evidence.quote: The task done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage
was decisive for twenty years to come. There was never a side-path of escape.
for himself an unknown ocean lay beyond. The generation that lived from 1840 to 1870

findings.minimal_repair: If space allows, restore the 'The task done...' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff within the 'pilotage' essential.
findings.reader_effect: Pilotage becomes a static image without its bitter cost, which quietly foreshadows the war generation. The father's candidacy is less tied to the boy's fixed road.
findings.title: Pilotage-payment irony and 'no side-path of escape' cut

findings.claim: In the source, 'He stood alone' concludes that Adams belonged to none of Boston's clergy, literary, or scientific circles. The first draft kept a compressed version. The revision deletes it and attaches the line to the analysis of his mental faculties.
findings.counterevidence: 'No master... no scholars' survives verbatim, and the line still reads sensibly.

evidence.quote: but Mr. Adams was not one of them; as a rule they were much too Websterian.
Mr. Adams cared very little for science. He stood alone.
Within its range it was a model. He stood alone. He had no master--hardly even his father.

findings.reader_effect: The isolation reads as temperamental rather than social and political. The 'Websterian' literary group contrast is lost.

findings.claim: The revision drops the sentence that makes the Free Soil party 'a chief influence in the education of the boy Henry in the six years 1848 to 1854,' affecting character 'when character is plastic.'
findings.counterevidence: Paragraph 13 still frames the library discussions as education, and the voice profile prizes exact dates.

findings.reader_effect: The chapter loses its explicit date frame and the step from father's party to the boy's education.
findings.title: Party-as-education bridge for 1848–1854 cut

remaining_concerns: The repair adds about 10 words and moves the draft further from the 3000-word target. Offsetting cuts are out of scope in this pass.

comment.original_text:
FAR back in childhood, among its earliest memories, Henry Adams could recall his first visit to Harvard College. He must have been nine years old when, on one of the singularly gloomy winter afternoons which beguiled Cambridgeport, his mother drove him out to visit his aunt, Mrs. Everett. Edward Everett was then President of the college and lived in the old President's House on Harvard Square. The boy remembered the drawing-room, on the left of the hall door, in which Mrs. Everett received them.

When Adams closed his interview with President Eliot, he asked the Bursar about his aunt's old drawing-room, for the house had been turned to base uses. The room and the deserted kitchen adjacent to it were to let. He took them. Above him, his brother Brooks, then a law student, had rooms, with a private staircase. Opposite was J. R. Dennett, a young instructor almost as literary as Adams himself, and more rebellious to conventions. The standard was below that of Washington, but it was, for the moment, the best.

For the next nine months the Assistant Professor had no time to waste on comforts or amusements. He exhausted all his strength in trying to keep one day ahead of his duties.

The two full Professors of History--Torrey and Gurney, charming men both--could not cover the ground. Between Gurney's classical courses and Torrey's modern ones, lay a gap of a thousand years, which Adams was expected to fill. The students had already elected courses numbered 1, 2, and 3, without knowing what was to be taught or who was to teach. If their new professor had asked what idea was in their minds, they must have replied that nothing at all was in their minds, since their professor had nothing in his, and down to the moment he took his chair and looked his scholars in the face, he had given, as far as he could remember, an hour, more or less, to the Middle Ages.

Not that his ignorance troubled him! He knew enough to be ignorant. His course had led him through oceans of ignorance; he had tumbled from one ocean into another till he had learned to swim; but even to him education was a serious thing. A parent gives life, but as parent, gives no more. A murderer takes life, but his deed stops there. A teacher affects eternity; he can never tell where his influence stops. A teacher must either treat history as a catalogue, a record, a romance, or as an evolution; and whether he affirms or denies evolution, he falls into all the burning faggots of the pit. In essence incoherent and immoral, history had either to be taught as such--or falsified.

Adams wanted to do neither. He had no theory of evolution to teach, and could not make the facts fit one. He knew that the man who should solve the riddle of the Middle Ages and bring them into the line of evolution from past to present, would be a greater man than Lamarck or Linnaeus; but history had nowhere broken down so pitiably, or avowed itself so hopelessly bankrupt, as there. History had lost even the sense of shame. For all serious purpose, it was less instructive than Walter Scott and Alexandre Dumas.

He could frankly tell the boys that, provided they passed their examinations, they might get their facts where they liked, and use the teacher only for questions. The only privilege a student had that was worth his claiming, was that of talking to the professor, and the professor was bound to encourage it. No man can instruct more than half-a-dozen students at once. The whole problem of education is one of its cost in money.

Barred from philosophy and bored by facts, he wanted to teach his students something not wholly useless. The number of students whose minds were of an order above the average was, in his experience, barely one in ten. All were respectable, and in the seven years of contact that lay before him, Adams was never to have cause to complain of one; but nine minds in ten take polish passively, like a hard surface; only the tenth sensibly reacts.

Adams thought that, as no one seemed to care what he did, he would try to cultivate this tenth mind, though necessarily at the expense of the other nine. He frankly acted on the rule that a teacher, who knew nothing of his subject, should not pretend to teach his scholars what he did not know, but should join them in trying to find the best way of learning it.

The task was doomed to failure for a reason which he could not control. Nothing is easier than to teach historical method, but, when learned, it has little use. History is a tangled skein that one may take up at any point, and break when one has unravelled enough; but complexity precedes evolution. The Pteraspis grins horribly from the closed entrance. He could think only of law as subject; the Law School as end; and he took, as victims of his experiment, half-a-dozen highly intelligent young men who seemed willing to work. The course began with the beginning, as far as the books showed a beginning in primitive man, and came down through the Salic Franks to the Norman English. Since no textbooks existed, the professor refused to profess, knowing no more than his students, and the students read what they pleased and compared their results. As pedagogy, nothing could be more triumphant. The boys worked like rabbits, and dug holes all over the field of archaic society; but their teacher knew from his own experience that his wonderful method led nowhere, and they would have to exert themselves to get rid of it in the Law School even more than they exerted themselves to acquire it in the college. Their science had no system, and could have none, since its subject was merely antiquarian.

What was the use of training an active mind to waste its energy? For himself he was clear that the fault lay in the system, which could lead only to inertia. Such little knowledge of himself as he possessed warranted him in affirming that his mind required conflict, competition, contradiction even more than that of the student. He would have seated a rival assistant professor opposite him, whose business should be strictly limited to expressing opposite views. Nothing short of this would ever interest either the professor or the student; but of all university freaks, no irregularity shocked the intellectual atmosphere so much as contradiction or competition between teachers.

He made use of his lost two years of German schooling to inflict their results on his students, and by a happy chance he was in the full tide of fashion. Germany was never so powerful, and the Assistant Professor of History had nothing else as his stock in trade. He imposed Germany on his scholars with a heavy hand. The seven years he was to pass in teaching would seem to him lost.

The uses of adversity are beyond measure strange. As a professor, he regarded himself as a failure. He regarded the system as wrong; more mischievous to the teachers than to the students; fallacious from the beginning to end. He was to quit the university at last, in 1877, with a feeling, that, if it had not been for the invariable courtesy and kindness shown by every one in it, from the President to the injured students, he should be sore at his failure.

These were his own feelings, but they seemed not to be felt in the college. John Fiske went so far in his notice of the family in "Appleton's Cyclopedia," as to say that Henry had left a great reputation at Harvard College; and Adams set the kind expression down to camaraderie. The case was different when President Eliot himself hinted that Adams's services merited recognition. Adams could have wept on his shoulder in hysterics, so grateful was he for the rare good-will that inspired the compliment; but he could not allow the college to think that he esteemed himself entitled to distinction. Yet nothing in the vanity of life struck him as more humiliating than that Harvard College, which he had persistently criticised, abused, abandoned, and neglected, should alone have offered him a dollar, an office, an encouragement, or a kindness. Harvard College might have its faults, but at least it redeemed America, since it was true to its own.

The only part of education that the professor thought a success was the students. He found them excellent company. Their faith in education was so full of pathos that one dared not ask them what they thought they could do with education when they got it. Adams did put the question to one of them, and was surprised at the answer: "The degree of Harvard College is worth money to me in Chicago." This reply upset his experience; for the degree of Harvard College had been rather a drawback to a young man in Boston and Washington. He still had to take for granted many things that they need not--among the rest, that his teaching did them more good than harm. In his own opinion the greatest good he could do them was to hold his tongue.

He never knew whether his colleagues shared his doubts about their own utility. Unlike himself, they knew more or less their business. Adams could not pretend that mediaeval society proved evolution; the Professor of Physics smiled at evolution. They knew what they had to teach; he did not. He could teach his students nothing; he was only educating himself at their cost.

The students alone satisfied. They thought they gained something. Perhaps they did. Adams fervently hoped that they might remain content; but supposing twenty years more to pass, and they should turn on him as fiercely as he had turned on his old instructors--what answer could he make? The college had pleaded guilty, and tried to reform. He had pleaded guilty from the start, and his reforms had failed before those of the college.

The lecture-room was futile enough, but the faculty-room was worse. Several score of the best-educated, most agreeable, and personally the most sociable people in America united in Cambridge to make a social desert that would have starved a polar bear. Society was a faculty-meeting without business.

Thus it turned out that of all his many educations, Adams thought that of school-teacher the thinnest. Yet he was forced to admit that the education of an editor, in some ways, was thinner still. The editor had barely time to edit; he had none to write. For seven years he was to write nothing; the Review lived on his brother Charles's railway articles. The secrets of success as an editor were easily learned; the highest was that of getting advertisements. Ten pages of advertising made an editor a success; five marked him as a failure.

A year or two of education as editor satiated most of his appetite for that career as a profession. On the whole, Adams preferred his attic in Washington. He was educated enough. Ignorance paid better, for at least it earned fifty dollars a month.

With this result Henry Adams's education, at his entry into life, stopped, and his life began. The editorship of the North American Review had one solitary merit; it made the editor acquainted at a distance with almost every one in the country who could write or who could be the cause of writing. Among these clever people, only one stood out in extraordinary prominence as the type and model of what Adams would have liked to be, and of what the American, as he conceived, should have been and was not.

Thanks to the article on Sir Charles Lyell, Adams passed for a friend of geologists. One of his friends from earliest childhood, and nearest neighbor in Quincy, Frank Emmons, had become a geologist and joined the Fortieth Parallel Survey under Government. At Washington in the winter of 1869-70, Emmons had invited Adams to go out with him on one of the field-parties in summer. When the first year of professing and editing was at last over, and his July North American appeared, he drew a long breath of relief, and took the next train for the West.

In the year 1871, the West was still fresh, and the Union Pacific was young. The topographers and geologists thought more about minerals than about Sioux. They felt the future in their hands.

Emmons's party was out of reach in the Uintahs, but Arnold Hague's had come in to Laramie for supplies, and they took charge of Adams for a time. One morning when the party was camped high above Estes Park, on the flank of Long's Peak, he borrowed a rod, and rode down over a rough trail into Estes Park, for some trout. Hour after hour the sun moved westward and the fish moved eastward, or disappeared altogether, until at last when the fisherman cinched his mule, sunset was nearer than he thought. Darkness caught him before he could catch his trail. Not caring to tumble into some fifty-foot hole, he "allowed" he was lost, and turned back. In half-an-hour he was out of the hills, and under the stars of Estes Park, but he saw no prospect of supper or of bed.

There was but one cabin in the Park, near its entrance, and he felt no great confidence in finding it, but he thought his mule cleverer than himself. The patient mule plodded on, and some two hours must have passed before a light showed in the distance. As the mule came up to the cabin door, two or three men came out to see the stranger.

One of these men was Clarence King on his way up to the camp. Adams fell into his arms. As with most friendships, it was never a matter of growth or doubt. Friends are born in archaic horizons; they were shaped with the Pteraspis in Siluria; they have nothing to do with the accident of space. King had come up that day from Greeley in a light four-wheeled buggy, over a trail hardly fit for a commissariat mule, as Adams had reason to know since he went back in the buggy. In the cabin, luxury provided a room and one bed for guests. They shared the room and the bed, and talked till far towards dawn.

King had everything to interest and delight Adams. He knew more than Adams did of art and poetry; he knew America, especially west of the hundredth meridian, better than any one; he knew the professor by heart, and he knew the Congressman better than he did the professor. Incidentally he knew more practical geology than was good for him, and saw ahead at least one generation further than the text-books. That he saw right was a different matter. Since the beginning of time no man has lived who is known to have seen right; the charm of King was that he saw what others did and a great deal more. One Clarence King only existed in the world.

A new friend is always a miracle, but at thirty-three years old, such a bird of paradise rising in the sage-brush was an avatar. One friend in a lifetime is much; two are many; three are hardly possible. Friendship needs a certain parallelism of life, a community of thought, a rivalry of aim.

King and the Fortieth Parallel influenced him in a way far more vital than charm. The lines of their lives converged, but King had moulded and directed his life logically, scientifically, as Adams thought American life should be directed. Standing in the middle of his career, he could look back and look forward on a straight line, with scientific knowledge for its base. Adams's life, past or future, was a succession of violent breaks or waves, with no base at all. King's abnormal energy had already won him great success. He was creating one of the classic scientific works of the century. Whatever prize he wanted lay ready for him--scientific social, literary, political--and he knew how to take them in turn. With ordinary luck he would die at eighty the richest and most many-sided genius of his day.

The young men of the Fortieth Parallel had Californian instincts; they were brothers of Bret Harte. They felt no leanings towards the simple uniformities of Lyell and Darwin; to them, catastrophe was the law of change. King loved paradox; he started them like rabbits, and cared for them no longer, when caught or lost; but they delighted Adams, for they helped to persuade him that history was more amusing than science. The only question left open to doubt was their relative money value.

In Emmons's camp, far up in the Uintahs, these talks were continued till the frosts became sharp in the mountains. No more education was possible for either man. Such as they were, they had got to stand the chances of the world they lived in; and when Adams started back to Cambridge, to take up again the humble tasks of schoolmaster and editor he was harnessed to his cart. Education, systematic or accidental, had done its worst. Henceforth, he went on, submissive.

evidence.quote: Adams could have wept on his shoulder in hysterics, so grateful was he for the rare good-will that inspired the compliment; but he could not allow the college to think that he esteemed himself entitled to distinction.
The case was different when President Eliot himself hinted that Adams's services merited recognition. Yet nothing in the vanity of life struck him as more humiliating

adjudications.reason: In the revision, 'The case was different' sets Eliot's compliment against the Fiske 'camaraderie' dismissal. Adams's grateful but self-denying response is cut, so 'Yet ... humiliating' follows the compliment directly. This misreads his attitude and breaks the turn. The plan's essential item on Fiske's and Eliot's praise requires the response.

evidence.quote: Nothing is easier than to teach historical method, but, when learned, it has little use.
Their science had no system, and could have none, since its subject was merely antiquarian.

adjudications.reason: The 'reason' still survives. The next sentence says the method, once learned, has little use, and the paragraph closes with the antiquarian explanation. The skein sentence and the Pteraspis grin deepen the point but are not needed for causality. The Pteraspis motif is kept in the protected V6. This is a legitimate tradeoff within the word budget.

evidence.quote: Nothing short of this would ever interest either the professor or the student; but of all university freaks, no irregularity shocked the intellectual atmosphere so much as contradiction or competition between teachers.

adjudications.reason: The plan item, the wish for a rival professor and for contradiction, is still met. The rival seated 'opposite him' and the line about contradiction between teachers survive, and 'interest either the professor or the student' keeps Adams's personal stake. The lost self-diagnosis is a nuance, not a break, so this is a reasonable cut given the budget.

evidence.quote: King's abnormal energy had already won him great success. He was creating one of the classic scientific works of the century.
Adams's life, past or future, was a succession of violent breaks or waves, with no base at all.

adjudications.reason: King's qualities survive: his knowledge, his far sight, and the 'saw what others did and a great deal more' line. His achievements also survive: great success, a classic scientific work, every prize ready to hand, and the protected prediction. The contrast with Adams's broken life is kept. The Alcibiades and Survey lines are enrichments, so cutting them is a valid tradeoff.

evidence.quote: The lines of their lives converged, but King had moulded and directed his life logically, scientifically, as Adams thought American life should be directed.

adjudications.reason: Paragraph 30 directly follows the friendship aphorism and supplies the parallelism with 'The lines of their lives converged' and the straight-line versus broken-waves contrast. The west/east sentence is ornamental, and its loss is an acceptable tradeoff.

findings.claim: The revision keeps 'The case was different' for Eliot's hint but cuts Adams's grateful, self-denying response. 'Yet ... humiliating' now follows directly, so the promised contrast with Fiske never arrives.
findings.counterevidence: Fiske's notice and its 'camaraderie' dismissal survive, so the contrast is half set up.

The portrait keeps King's knowledge, his seeing further than others, and 'One Clarence King only existed'. The essential is met. Restoring about 50 words would cost more than the target allows, so this is an artistic tradeoff rather than a necessary repair.

The first draft already dropped the stationary-consumption sentence, leaving 'this stationary period' without its antecedent. The revision further cuts the generations dying in that faith, 'This mental inertia of science', and the authorities' continued resistance.

The chapter's inertia law ('inertia almost invariably has ended in tragedy') is no longer turned against science itself. The irony that the scientists were the inert mass breaks, and the Mill reference floats.

comment.original_text:
IMAGES are not arguments, rarely even lead to proof, but the mind craves them, and, of late more than ever, the keenest experimenters find twenty images better than one, especially if contradictory; since the human mind has already learned to deal in contradictions.

The image needed here is that of a new centre, or preponderating mass, artificially introduced on earth in the midst of a system of attractive forces that previously made their own equilibrium, and constantly induced to accelerate its motion till it shall establish a new equilibrium. A dynamic theory would begin by assuming that all history, terrestrial or cosmic, mechanical or intellectual, would be reducible to this formula if we knew the facts.

The simplest figure is that of a perfect comet--say that of 1843--which drops from space, in a straight line, at the regular acceleration of speed, directly into the sun, and after wheeling sharply about it, in heat that ought to dissipate any known substance, turns back unharmed, in defiance of law, by the path on which it came. The mind, by analogy, may figure as such a comet, the better because it also defies law.

Motion is the ultimate object of science, and measures of motion are many; but with thought as with matter, the true measure is mass in its astronomic sense--the sum or difference of attractive forces. Especially in the nineteenth century, society by common accord agreed in measuring its progress by the coal-output. The ratio of increase in the volume of coal-power may serve as dynamometer.

The coal-output of the world, speaking roughly, doubled every ten years between 1840 and 1900, in the form of utilized power, for the ton of coal yielded three or four times as much power in 1900 as in 1840. Perhaps the ocean steamer is nearest unity and easiest to measure, for any one might hire, in 1905, the use of 30,000 steam-horse-power to cross the ocean, and by halving this figure every ten years, he got back to 234 horse-power for 1835, which was accuracy enough for his purposes. In truth, his chief trouble came not from the ratio in volume of heat, but from the intensity, since he could get no basis for a ratio there. Within ten years a new universe of force had been revealed in radiation. At all events, the ten-year ratio seemed carefully conservative.

Thus, taking the year 1900 as the starting point for carrying back the series, nothing was easier than to assume a ten-year period of retardation as far back as 1820, but beyond that point the statistician failed, and only the mathematician could help. Laplace would have found it child's-play to fix a ratio of progression in mathematical science between Descartes, Leibnitz, Newton, and himself. No one in 1789 doubted the progress of force, least of all those who were to lose their heads by it.

Pending agreement between these authorities, theory may assume what it likes--say a fifty, or even a five-and-twenty-year period of reduplication for the eighteenth century, for the period matters little until the acceleration itself is admitted. A historian might be tempted to maintain a similar rate of movement back to 1600, and, to save trouble, might tentatively carry back the same ratio to the year 1400, with the help of Columbus and Gutenberg, leaving to statisticians the task of correcting it.

Or better, one might, for convenience, use the formula of squares to serve for a law of mind. As the human meteoroid approached the sun or centre of attractive force, the attraction of one century squared itself to give the measure of attraction in the next.

Behind the year 1400, the process certainly went on, but the progress became so slight as to be hardly measurable. An architect might detect a sequence between St. Peter's, Amiens, and the churches at Ravenna. All the historian dares affirm is that a sequence is manifestly there, and he has a right to carry back his ratio, to represent the fact, without assuming its numerical correctness. On the human mind as a moving body, the break in acceleration in the Middle Ages is only apparent; the attraction worked through shifting forms of force, but with invariable law.

The science of prehistoric man has no value except to prove that the law went back into indefinite antiquity. A stone arrowhead is as convincing as a steam-engine. The motion at last became infinitely slight, but cannot be proved to have stopped. To historians the single interest is the law of reaction between force and force--between mind and nature--the law of progress.

The great division of history into phases by Turgot and Comte first affirmed this law in its outlines by asserting the unity of progress, for a mere phase interrupts no growth. The development of coal-power in the nineteenth century furnished the first means of assigning closer values to the elements; and the appearance of supersensual forces towards 1900 made this calculation a pressing necessity.

A law of acceleration, definite and constant as any law of mechanics, cannot be supposed to relax its energy to suit the convenience of man. In every age man has bitterly and justly complained that Nature hurried and hustled him, for inertia almost invariably has ended in tragedy. Resistance is its law, and resistance to superior mass is futile and fatal.

Fifty years ago, science took for granted that the rate of acceleration could not last. Two generations, with John Stuart Mill, talked of this stationary period, which was to follow the explosion of new power. Nothing short of radium fairly wakened men to the fact, long since evident, that force was inexhaustible.

Nothing so revolutionary had happened since the year 300. Power leaped from every atom. Man could no longer hold it off. Forces grasped his wrists and flung him about as though he had hold of a live wire or a runaway automobile; which was very nearly the exact truth for the purposes of an elderly and timid single gentleman in Paris, who never drove down the Champs Elysees without expecting an accident, and commonly witnessing one; or found himself in the neighborhood of an official without calculating the chances of a bomb. So long as the rates of progress held good, these bombs would double in force and number every ten years.

One's life had fattened on impossibilities. Before the boy was six years old, he had seen four impossibilities made actual--the ocean-steamer, the railway, the electric telegraph, and the Daguerreotype. He had seen the coal-output of the United States grow from nothing to three hundred million tons or more. What was far more serious, he had seen the number of minds, engaged in pursuing force--the truest measure of its attraction--increase from a few scores or hundreds, in 1838, to many thousands in 1905. Every day Nature violently revolted, causing so-called accidents with enormous destruction of property and life, while plainly laughing at man. The railways alone approached the carnage of war. An immense volume of force had detached itself from the unknown universe of energy, while still vaster reservoirs, supposed to be infinite, steadily revealed themselves.

If a perplexed but laborious follower could venture to guess the drift of men of science in 1900, it seemed in their minds a toss-up between anarchy and order. If Karl Pearson's notions of the universe were sound, men like Galileo, Descartes, Leibnitz, and Newton should have stopped the progress of science before 1700, supposing them to have been honest in the religious convictions they expressed. In 1900 they were plainly forced back; on faith in a unity unproved and an order they had themselves disproved. If any analogy whatever existed between the human mind and the laws of motion, the mind had already entered a field of attraction so violent that it must immediately pass beyond, into new equilibrium, like the Comet of Newton, to suffer dissipation altogether, like meteoroids in the earth's atmosphere. If it behaved like an explosive, it must rapidly recover equilibrium; if it behaved like a vegetable, it must reach its limits of growth; and even if it acted like the earlier creations of energy--the saurians and sharks--it must have nearly reached the limits of its expansion. An average mind had succumbed already in 1850; it could no longer understand the problem in 1900.

Fortunately, a student of history had no responsibility for the problem; he took it as science gave it, and waited only to be taught. For the American of the twentieth century, a historian asked no longer to be teacher or even friend; he asked only to be a pupil, and promised to be docile, for once, even though trodden under foot; for he could see that the new American--the child of incalculable coal-power, chemical power, electric power, and radiating energy--must be a sort of God compared with any former creation of nature. At the rate of progress since 1800, every American who lived into the year 2000 would know how to control unlimited power. To him the nineteenth century would stand on the same plane with the fourth--equally childlike. Perhaps even he might go back, in 1964, to sit with Gibbon on the steps of Ara Coeli.

Meanwhile he was getting education. The new forces would educate. The attempt of the American of 1800 to educate the American of 1900 had not often been surpassed for folly; and the attempt of the American of 1900 to educate the American of 2000, must be even blinder, except so far as he had learned his ignorance. The teacher of 1900, if foolhardy, might stimulate; if foolish, might resist; if intelligent, might balance; but the forces would continue to educate, and the mind would continue to react. All the teacher could hope was to teach it reaction.

Even there his difficulty was extreme. The most elementary books of science betrayed the inadequacy of old implements of thought. Chapter after chapter closed with phrases such as one never met in older literature: "The cause of this phenomenon is not understood"; "science gets on only by adopting different theories, sometimes contradictory." Evidently the new American would need to think in contradictions, and instead of Kant's famous four antinomies, the new universe would know no law that could not be proved by its anti-law.

To educate--one's self to begin with--had been the effort of one's life for sixty years; and the difficulties of education had gone on doubling with the coal-output, until the prospect of waiting another ten years, in order to face a seventh doubling of complexities, allured one's imagination but slightly. The movement from unity into multiplicity, between 1200 and 1900, was unbroken in sequence, and rapid in acceleration. Prolonged one generation longer, it would require a new social mind. Thus far, since five or ten thousand years, the mind had successfully reacted, and nothing yet proved that it would fail to react--but it would need to jump.
