comment.original_text:
A DYNAMIC theory, like most theories, begins by begging the question: it defines Progress as the development and economy of Forces. Further, it defines force as anything that does, or helps to do work. Man is a force; so is the sun; so is a mathematical point, though without dimensions or known existence.

Man commonly begs the question again taking for granted that he captures the forces. A dynamic theory, assigning attractive force to opposing bodies in proportion to the law of mass, takes for granted that the forces of nature capture man. The sum of force attracts; the feeble atom or molecule called man is attracted; he suffers education or growth; he is the sum of the forces that attract him; his body and his thought are alike their product.

For convenience as an image, the theory may liken man to a spider in its web, watching for chance prey. Forces of nature dance like flies before the net, and the spider pounces on them when it can; but it makes many fatal mistakes, though its theory of force is sound. Man had acute sensibility to the higher forces. Fire taught him secrets that no other animal could learn; running water probably taught him even more, especially in his first lessons of mechanics; the animals helped to educate him, carrying his burdens or supplying his clothing; the grasses and grains were academies of study.

Long before history began, his education was complete. The universe that had formed him took shape in his mind as a reflection of his own unity, containing all forces except himself. Susceptibility to the highest forces is the highest genius; selection between them is the highest science; their mass is the highest educator. Man always made, and still makes, grotesque blunders in selecting and measuring forces, taken at random from the heap, but he never made a mistake in the value he set on the whole, which he symbolized as unity and worshipped as God. To this day, his attitude towards it has never changed, though science can no longer give to force a name.

Man's function as a force of nature was to assimilate other forces as he assimilated food. He called it the love of power. He felt his own feebleness, and he sought for an ass or a camel, a bow or a sling, to widen his range of power, as he sought fetish or a planet in the world beyond.

To the highest attractive energy, man gave the name of divine, and for its control he invented the science called Religion, a word which meant, and still means, cultivation of occult force whether in detail or mass. Hunger, whether for food or for the infinite, sets in motion multiplicity and infinity of thought, and the sure hope of gaining a share of infinite power in eternal life would lift most minds to effort.

He had reached this completeness five thousand years ago, and added nothing to his stock of known forces for a very long time. Such progress as the world made consisted in economies of energy rather than in its development; it was proved in mathematics; or in Civil Law, measured by a number of names which Adams had begun life by failing to learn; or in roads, or the size of ships, or harbors; all of them economies of force; but the roads were still travelled by the horse, the ass, the camel, or the slave; the ships were still propelled by sails or oars; the lever, the spring, and the screw bounded the region of applied mechanics. Even the metals were old.

Much the same thing could be said of religious or supernatural forces. Down to the year 300 of the Christian era they were little changed, and in spite of Plato and the sceptics were more apparently chaotic than ever.

There the Western world stood till the year A.D. 305, when the Emperor Diocletian abdicated; and there it was that Adams broke down on the steps of Ara Coeli, his path blocked by the scandalous failure of civilization at the moment it had achieved complete success. In the year 305 the empire had solved the problems of Europe more completely than they have ever been solved since.

The efforts to explain, or explain away, this scandal had been incessant, but none suited Adams unless it were the economic theory of adverse exchanges and exhaustion of minerals; but nations are not ruined beyond a certain point by adverse exchanges, and Rome had by no means exhausted her resources. On the contrary, the empire developed resources and energies quite astounding; in northwestern Europe alone it had developed three energies--France, England, and Germany--competent to master the world. The trouble seemed rather to be that the empire developed too much energy, and too fast.

The theory seems to exact excess, rather than deficiency, of action and reaction to account for the dissolution of the Roman Empire, which should, as a problem of mechanics, have been torn to pieces by acceleration. With the relentless logic that stamped Roman thought, the empire, which had established unity on earth, could not help establishing unity in heaven. It was induced by its dynamic necessities to economize the gods.

Good taste forbids saying that Constantine the Great speculated as audaciously as a modern stock-broker on values of which he knew at the utmost only the volume; or that he merged all uncertain forces into a single trust, which he enormously overcapitalized, and forced on the market; but this is the substance of what Constantine himself said in his Edict of Milan in the year 313, which admitted Christianity into the Trust of State Religions. Regarded as an Act of Congress, it runs: "We have resolved to grant to Christians as well as all others the liberty to practice the religion they prefer, in order that whatever exists of divinity or celestial power may help and favor us and all who are under our government." The empire pursued power--not merely spiritual but physical--in the sense in which Constantine issued his army order the year before, at the battle of the Milvian Bridge: In hoc signo vinces! using the Cross as a train of artillery, which, to his mind, it was. Eighty years afterwards, Theodosius marched against his rival Eugene with the Cross for physical champion; while society on both sides looked on, as though it were a boxing-match. The laity, the people, the million, almost to a man, bet on the gods as they bet on a horse.

No doubt the Church did all it could to purify the process, but society was almost wholly pagan in its point of view, and was drawn to the Cross because, in its system of physics, the Cross had absorbed all the old occult or fetish-power. The symbol represented the sum of nature--the Energy of modern science--and society believed it to be as real as X-rays; perhaps it was!

Fetish-power was cheap and satisfactory, down to a certain point. Outside of it, the Roman world was incredibly poor. It knew but one productive energy resembling a modern machine--the slave. When society developed itself so rapidly in political and social lines, it had no other means of keeping its economy on the same level than to extend its slave-system and its fetish-system to the utmost. The economic needs of a violently centralizing society forced the empire to enlarge its slave-system until the slave-system consumed itself and the empire too, leaving society no resource but further enlargement of its religious system in order to compensate for the losses and horrors of the failure. For a vicious circle, its mathematical completeness approached perfection.

At last, in 410, Alaric sacked Rome, and the slave-ridden, agricultural, uncommercial Western Empire--the poorer and less Christianized half--went to pieces. The outcry against the Cross became so loud among Christians that Bishop Augustine of Hippo was led to write a famous treatise in defence of the Cross, in which he defended feebly the mechanical value of the symbol--arguing only that pagan symbols equally failed--but insisted on its spiritual value in the Civitas Dei which had taken the place of the Civitas Romae in human interest. "Granted that we have lost all we had! Have we lost faith? Have we lost piety? Have we lost the wealth of the inner man who is rich before God? These are the wealth of Christians!" St. Augustine and his people perished at Hippo towards 430, leaving society in appearance dull to new attraction.

Yet the attraction remained constant. Never has Nature offered the mind so violent a stimulant as when she opened to it the possibility of sharing infinite power in eternal life, and it might well need a thousand years of intense experiment to prove the value of the motive. During these so-called Middle Ages, the Western mind expressed its motives in Romanesque and Gothic architecture, glass windows and mosaic walls, sculpture and poetry, war and love, which still affect some people as the noblest work of man, so that tourists travel from far countries to look at Ravenna and San Marco, Chartres, with vague notions about the force that created them.

The tourist more rarely visits Constantinople or studies the architecture of Sancta Sofia, but when he does, he is distinctly conscious of forces not quite the same. The dynamic scheme began by asserting rather recklessly that between the Pyramids (B.C. 3000), and the Cross (A.D. 300), no new force affected Western progress, and antiquarians may easily dispute the fact; but in any case the motive which raised both Pyramids and Cross was the same attraction of power in a future life that raised the dome of Sancta Sofia and the Cathedral at Amiens. Therefore, no single event has more puzzled historians than the sudden, unexplained appearance of at least two new natural forces of the highest educational value in mechanics.

Of the compass one may confidently say that it proved, better than any other force, the widening scope of the mind, since it widened immensely the range of contact between nature and thought. The compass educated.

Of Greek fire and gunpowder, the same thing cannot certainly be said, for they have the air of accidents due to the attraction of religious motives. They were chemical forces, mostly explosives, which acted and still act as the most violent educators ever known to man, but they were justly feared as diabolic, and man was an abject pupil towards explosives. The Sieur de Joinville left a record of the energy with which the relatively harmless Greek fire educated the French mind in a single night in the year 1249. The good king St. Louis and all his staff dropped on their knees at every fiery flame that flew by, praying--"God have pity on us!" and never had man more reason to call on his gods than they, for the battle of religion between Christian and Saracen was trifling compared with that of education between gunpowder and the Cross.

The fiction that society educated itself, or aimed at a conscious purpose, was upset by the compass and gunpowder which dragged and drove Europe at will through frightful bogs of learning. When the Crescent drove the Cross in ignominy from Constantinople in 1453, Gutenberg and Fust were printing their first Bible at Mainz under the impression that they were helping the Cross. When Luther and Calvin upset Europe half a century later, they were trying, like St. Augustine, to substitute the Civitas Dei for the Civitas Romae. When the Puritans set out for New England in 1620, they too were looking to found a Civitas Dei in State Street. Even when the Church burned Giordano Bruno in 1600, besides condemning Galileo in 1630, it condemned anarchists, not atheists. Neither Galileo nor Kepler, neither Spinoza nor Descartes, neither Leibnitz nor Newton, any more than Constantine the Great--if so much--doubted Unity. The utmost range of their heresies reached only its personality.

This persistence of thought-inertia is the leading idea of modern history. Except as reflected in himself, man has no reason for assuming unity in the universe, or an ultimate substance, or a prime-motor. The a priori insistence on this unity ended by fatiguing the more active--or reactive--minds; and Lord Bacon tried to stop it. He urged society to lay aside the idea of evolving the universe from a thought, and to try evolving thought from the universe. "Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed." As Galileo reversed the action of earth and sun, Bacon reversed the relation of thought to force. The mind was thenceforth to follow the movement of matter, and unity must be left to shift for itself.

The revolution in attitude seemed voluntary, but in fact was as mechanical as the fall of a feather. Man created nothing. After 1500, the speed of progress so rapidly surpassed man's gait as to alarm every one, as though it were the acceleration of a falling body which the dynamic theory takes it to be. The telescope held society rigidly standing on its head; gunpowder killed whole races that lagged behind; the compass coerced the most imbruted mariner to act on the impossible idea that the earth was round; the press drenched Europe with anarchism. Europe's resistance was often bloody, sometimes humorous, always constant; and still, throughout it all, the Baconian law held good; thought did not evolve nature, but nature evolved thought. The whole number of those who acted, like Franklin, as electric conductors of the new forces from nature to man, down to the year 1800, did not exceed a few score, confined to a few towns in western Europe.

The success of this method staggers belief. Evidently a new variety of mind had appeared. Certain men merely held out their hands--like Newton, watched an apple; like Franklin, flew a kite; like Watt, played with a tea-kettle--and great forces of nature stuck to them as though she were playing ball.

The influx of new force was nearly spontaneous; and had it stopped in Europe, society must have stood still, or gone backward, as in Asia or Africa. Then only economies of process would have counted as new force, and society would have been better pleased; for the idea that new force must be in itself a good is only an animal or vegetable instinct. As Nature developed her hidden energies, they tended to become destructive. Thought itself became tortured, suffering reluctantly, impatiently, painfully, the coercion of new method.

The stupendous acceleration after 1800 ended in 1900 with the appearance of the new class of supersensual forces, before which the man of science stood at first as bewildered and helpless as, in the fourth century, a priest of Isis before the Cross of Christ.

This, then, or something like this, would be a dynamic formula of history. Any schoolboy knows enough to object at once that it is the oldest and most universal of all theories. Whether the attractive energy has been called God or Nature, the mechanism has been always the same, and history is not obliged to decide whether the Ultimate tends to a purpose or not, or whether ultimate energy is one or many. There is nothing unscientific in the idea that, beyond the lines of force felt by the senses, the universe may be--as it has always been--either a supersensuous chaos or a divine unity, which irresistibly attracts, and is either life or death to penetrate. Thus far, religion, philosophy, and science seem to go hand in hand. The schools begin their vital battle only there. As the mind of man enlarged its range, it enlarged the field of complexity, and must continue to do so, even into chaos, until the reservoirs of sensuous or supersensuous energies are exhausted, or cease to affect him, or until he succumbs to their excess.

For past history, this way of grouping its sequences may answer for a chart of relations, although any serious student would need to invent another, to compare or correct its errors; but past history is only a value of relation to the future, and this value is wholly one of convenience, which can be tested only by experiment. Any law of movement must include, to make it a convenience, some mechanical formula of acceleration.

pipeline_review.body: 7 edits across 3 editorial passes. Review the current chapter and the recorded before/after changes. Any outstanding critic findings are listed separately.

evidence.quote: Long before history began, his education was complete
He had reached this completeness five thousand years ago

adjudications.reason: The revision cuts the sentence stating that man's education was complete before history began. Nothing else in revision p4–p6 states a finished state. As a result, p7's 'this completeness' has no antecedent. The early-teachers list in p3 describes a process, not its completion. Restoring the short main clause repairs the referent.

evidence.quote: It was induced by its dynamic necessities to economize the gods.
using the Cross as a train of artillery, which, to his mind, it was.

adjudications.reason: Cutting this frame is a legitimate tradeoff. The essentials that survive are the trust conceit (V4), the Edict quoted as an Act of Congress, and the Cross used as artillery. Revision p11 ends on 'economize the gods,' which leads straight into the Constantine passage. The Cross is named as the attracting force in p12 and p13. P13's 'No doubt the Church did all it could' still reads coherently without the earlier concession.

evidence.quote: Fetish-power was cheap and satisfactory, down to a certain point.
The economic needs of a violently centralizing society forced the empire to enlarge its slave-system until the slave-system consumed itself and the empire too

adjudications.reason: The mechanism of collapse survives. The draft still says fetish was cheap, the slave was the only machine, and centralization forced the slave-system to consume itself and the empire. It then names the vicious circle. The planned essential is met, and the lost sentences are elaboration.

evidence.quote: leaving society in appearance dull to new attraction.
insisted on its spiritual value in the Civitas Dei

adjudications.reason: 'Yet the attraction remained constant' has a clear referent: it answers the end of p15, 'dull to new attraction.' Augustine's spiritual value 'in the Civitas Dei' carries the transfer of attraction. The later Luther and Puritan echoes of the Civitas Dei therefore still resolve.

evidence.quote: For convenience as an image
The dynamic scheme began by asserting rather recklessly

adjudications.reason: The plan names the hedges 'for convenience' and 'rather recklessly,' and both survive (p3, p17, p27). The deleted assimilation sentence was itself the speculation. Removing it does not turn any speculation into asserted fact. The dating disclaimer qualified a claim the revision no longer makes.

evidence.quote: Europe saw itself, violently resisting
the press drenched Europe with anarchism. The resistance was often bloody

adjudications.reason: Every mention of society or Europe resisting has been cut from p20 and p22. 'The resistance' therefore has no stated agent. The essential 'resistance is constant' depends on the reader knowing who resists. A zero-word local edit naming Europe, which appears in the preceding clause, repairs the referent without padding.

findings.claim: The revision deletes 'Long before history began, his education was complete'. The first draft had kept it, and the 'highest powers early' clause was already gone. Paragraph 7 still opens 'He had reached this completeness five thousand years ago,' which now refers to nothing.
findings.counterevidence: Revision p3 lists man's early teachers, so a reader may vaguely infer a completed education.

evidence.quote: Long before history began, his education was complete, for the record could not have been started until he had been taught to record.
Long before history began, his education was complete, for the record could not have been started until he had been taught to record.
He had reached this completeness five thousand years ago, and added nothing to his stock of known forces for a very long time.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the opening sentence of source p4 at the head of revision p4.
findings.plan_relation: Required by the 'man's early teachers' essential. This is a dangling residue of a cut.
findings.reader_effect: The prehistoric-education premise is the base of the stasis argument (no new force for millennia). Without it, the dating claim reads as a non sequitur.
findings.title: "This completeness" left without antecedent

findings.claim: The revision drops the opening of source p12, which the first draft had kept. That opening has the Church denying that Christianity ruined the empire, the theory 'gladly' admitting it, and the decision to follow the force the Church itself points to in the Cross. The paragraph now jumps from 'economize the gods' to 'Good taste forbids.'
findings.counterevidence: Revision p11's 'economize the gods' supplies a minimal transition, and V4/V5 survive intact.

evidence.quote: Any dynamic theory gladly admits it. All it asks is to find and follow the force that attracts.
The Church points out this force in the Cross, and history needs only to follow it.
Good taste forbids saying that Constantine the Great speculated as audaciously as a modern stock-broker

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'Any dynamic theory gladly admits it. All it asks is to find and follow the force that attracts. The Church points out this force in the Cross, and history needs only to follow it.' with a short lead-in clause about the Church's protest.
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff not authorized by the plan. The plan does not list this frame for cutting.
findings.reader_effect: Adams's dialectical irony is lost: he concedes the Church's case in order to turn it into dynamics. The Cross also enters the argument without being named as the attracting force. The stock-broker conceit loses its setup, and p13's 'No doubt the Church did all it could' loses its counterpart.
findings.title: Church's protest and the theory's ironic concession cut

findings.claim: The revision cuts three links the first draft kept. One is the instruction to assign values to the forces of attraction 'in plain evidence'. Another is the hiring of 'an occult force at trifling expense'. The third is rapid political development forcing extension of the slave and fetish systems. 'Too much energy, too fast' no longer connects to the vicious circle.
findings.counterevidence: 'Violently centralizing society' and the vicious-circle sentence still imply the mechanism.

evidence.quote: no one could afford to buy or construct a costly and complicated machine when he could hire an occult force at trifling expense.

when society developed itself so rapidly in political and social lines, it had no other means of keeping its economy on the same level than to extend its slave-system and its fetish-system to the utmost.
No one could afford to buy or construct a costly and complicated machine when he could hire an occult force at trifling expense.
Fetish-power was cheap and satisfactory, down to a certain point. Outside of it, the Roman world was incredibly poor.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'hire an occult force at trifling expense' sentence before 'Fetish-power was cheap.' Optionally restore the 'developed itself so rapidly' clause.
findings.plan_relation: Required by the 'Slave and fetish as Rome's only engines; the vicious circle' essential.
findings.reader_effect: The theory's one worked example becomes a series of claims. The reader loses why fetish was preferred to machines and why rapid growth drove the circle.
findings.title: Rome's mechanism of collapse thinned to assertion

findings.claim: The revision cuts society's disappointment that the Cross 'failed to protect its Church'. It also cuts the sentence making the Civitas Dei the new 'sum of attraction' with the same mechanical weakness. Both were in the first draft. 'Yet the attraction remained constant' now lacks its referent.
findings.counterevidence: 'Outcry against the Cross' implies disappointment, and Augustine's 'spiritual value in the Civitas Dei' partly carries the transfer.

evidence.quote: The Civitas Dei, in its turn, became the sum of attraction for the Western world, though it also showed the same weakness in mechanics that had wrecked the Civitas Romae.
Society felt still more deeply the disappointment in its new power, the Cross, which had failed to protect its Church.
went to pieces. The outcry against the Cross became so loud among Christians
Yet the attraction remained constant.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the Civitas Dei 'sum of attraction' sentence before 'St. Augustine and his people perished.'
findings.plan_relation: Required by the 'Augustine's defence of spiritual over mechanical value' essential.
findings.reader_effect: The Cross is no longer judged as failed mechanical power, which is the dynamic point of the passage. The handoff to the Middle Ages and to later Civitas Dei echoes (Luther, the Puritans) weakens.
findings.title: Augustine aftermath loses cause and the Civitas Dei transfer

findings.claim: The first draft kept both qualifications. The revision deletes 'Nothing forbids one to admit, for convenience, that the mind may assimilate food like the body.' It also deletes 'Only a historian of very exceptional knowledge would venture to say' when Europe's momentum peaked.
findings.counterevidence: 'For convenience' survives in p3 and p27, and 'rather recklessly' survives in p17.

evidence.quote: nothing forbids one to admit, for convenience, that it may assimilate food like the body, storing new force and growing, like a forest, with the storage.
Nothing forbids one to admit, for convenience, that the mind may assimilate food like the body
Yet the attraction remained constant. Never has Nature offered the mind so violent a stimulant
Only a historian of very exceptional knowledge would venture to say at what date between 3000 B.C. and 1000 A.D., the momentum of Europe was greatest

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'for convenience' assimilation sentence in revision p16.
findings.plan_relation: The continuity check asks to keep the 'for convenience' hedges.
findings.reader_effect: Speculative analogies now read as plainer assertion. Adams's characteristic hedged prophecy is thinned, and the assimilation thread from p5 loses its continuation.
findings.title: Required 'for convenience' hedge and dating disclaimer removed

findings.claim: The revision removes 'Europe saw itself, violently resisting... as a fish that is caught on a hook' and the 'dragged into situations' sentence, both kept in the first draft. 'The resistance was often bloody' now follows the instrument list with no stated resister.
findings.counterevidence: 'Alarm every one' and 'held society rigidly standing on its head' imply resistance.

evidence.quote: Europe saw itself, violently resisting, wrenched into false positions, drawn along new lines as a fish that is caught on a hook
Europe saw itself, violently resisting, drawn along new lines as a fish that is caught on a hook
the press drenched Europe with anarchism. The resistance was often bloody, sometimes humorous, always constant

findings.minimal_repair: Reinsert the first draft's 'Europe saw itself, violently resisting...' sentence before 'The resistance was often bloody.'
findings.plan_relation: Required by the 'resistance is constant' essential.
findings.reader_effect: This weakens the planned point that resistance is constant and involuntary. It also loses the fish-on-hook image of capture, which echoes the man-captured-by-forces inversion.
findings.title: "The resistance" dangles after Europe's resistance is cut

findings.claim: Two sentences the first draft kept are cut. One states that the Eastern Empire showed a variety of forces classical Europe never had. The other states that the new forces appeared at the moment Cross and Crescent proclaimed the Civitas Dei's triumph.
findings.counterevidence: 'Sudden, unexplained appearance' and the gunpowder-versus-Cross line in p19 retain part of the irony.

evidence.quote: Literally, these two forces seemed to drop from the sky at the precise moment when the Cross on one side and the Crescent on the other, proclaimed the complete triumph of the Civitas Dei.
The Eastern Empire showed an activity and variety of forces that classical Europe had never possessed.
he is distinctly conscious of forces not quite the same. The dynamic scheme began by asserting rather recklessly

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'Eastern Empire showed an activity and variety' sentence. Optionally restore the 'drop from the sky' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: Essential lists 'Byzantium shows more varied forces'; only the tourist list and navy were marked compressible.
findings.reader_effect: The planned Byzantium contrast shrinks to 'forces not quite the same.' The ironic timing that sets new mechanical force against religious triumph is lost.
findings.title: Byzantine variety and the 'dropped from the sky' irony cut

findings.claim: The revision drops 'Church and State, theology and philosophy, have always preached it,' which the first draft had kept. The schoolboy objection now rests on assertion alone.
findings.counterevidence: 'God or Nature... the mechanism has been always the same' partly substitutes for it.

findings.plan_relation: Supports the essential 'formula admitted to be the oldest theory'.
findings.reader_effect: The admission loses its evidence, so the turn from historical sweep to universal mechanism is less earned.

adjudications.reason: Paragraph 10 ends on 'too much energy, and too fast.' Paragraph 14 then jumps from 'the slave' straight to the slave-system consuming itself. The source sentence that ties rapid political and social growth to extending both the slave-system and the fetish-system is gone. That sentence is the middle step of the vicious circle, which the plan lists as essential. 'Violently centralizing' only partly covers it.

evidence.quote: the sudden, unexplained appearance of at least two new natural forces of the highest educational value in mechanics.
to substitute the Civitas Dei for the Civitas Romae

adjudications.reason: The essential 'sudden arrival' survives as 'sudden, unexplained appearance.' The Civitas Dei is still introduced through Augustine and reused for Luther and the Puritans. The ironic timing at religion's triumph is lost, but restoring it would cost 34 words. The fixed budget cannot absorb that without cutting essential material, so this is a defensible tradeoff.

evidence.quote: The revolution in attitude seemed voluntary, but in fact was as mechanical as the fall of a feather. Man created nothing.
Europe's resistance was often bloody, sometimes humorous, always constant

adjudications.reason: Resistance is not abrupt. It follows directly on concrete coercions: the telescope, gunpowder, the compass and the press. Constant resistance is stated outright, and involuntariness is set up by 'as mechanical as the fall of a feather' and 'Man created nothing.' The fish image is ornamental, so cutting it is a legitimate tradeoff.

evidence.quote: Whether the attractive energy has been called God or Nature, the mechanism has been always the same
either a supersensuous chaos or a divine unity, which irresistibly attracts, and is either life or death to penetrate. Thus far, religion, philosophy, and science seem to go hand in hand.

adjudications.reason: The 'oldest and most universal of all theories' admission is still there. 'God or Nature' with the same mechanism supplies the convergence. The chaos-or-unity alternative directly precedes 'hand in hand' and 'The schools begin their vital battle only there,' so the essential divergence at the edge remains argued.

findings.claim: The revision cuts two sentences the first draft kept. One explains that no one would buy a machine when occult force was cheap. The other explains that rapid political growth forced Rome to extend both slave-system and fetish-system. 'Fetish-power was cheap' now lacks its comparison, and the vicious circle no longer ties back to 'too much energy, and too fast.'
findings.counterevidence: The slave-system sentence and 'vicious circle' survive, so the outline remains readable.

comment.author: Pipeline critic
comment.body:
The revision drops several of Adams's closers and images that the first draft kept: 'For weeks he lived in silence', 'In this case, the contradiction seemed crude', 'He seemed bent on crushing rivalry'. It also cuts the Civil War drill that motivates 'shouldered his pack' and the 'drifted as attraction offered itself' line that seeds the attraction motif.

Paragraph cadence flattens, and the attraction metaphor arrives at the end with less preparation.

Restore 'For weeks he lived in silence.' and the drifting-by-attraction sentence.
comment.original_text:
The summer of the Spanish War began the Indian summer of life to one who had reached sixty years of age, and cared only to reap in peace such harvest as these sixty years had yielded. In London, in 1898, the scene was singularly interesting to the last survivor of the Legation of 1861. He carried every scene of it, in a century and a half since the Stamp Act, quite alive in his mind--all the interminable disputes of his disputatious ancestors--as well as his own insignificance in the Civil War, every step in which had the object of bringing England into an American system. For this they had written libraries of argument and remonstrance, and had piled war on war; and suddenly, by pure chance, the blessing fell on Hay, now American Ambassador in London. Hay himself scarcely knew how grateful he should be, for to him the change came almost of course; but to Adams, still living in the atmosphere of Palmerston and John Russell, the sudden appearance of Germany as the grizzly terror which, in twenty years effected what Adamses had tried for two hundred in vain--frightened England into America's arms--seemed as melodramatic as any plot of Napoleon the Great. He could feel only the sense of satisfaction at seeing the diplomatic triumph of all his family, since the breed existed, at last realized under his own eyes for the advantage of his oldest and closest ally.

This was history, not education, yet it taught something exceedingly serious, if not ultimate, could one trust the lesson. For the first time in his life, he felt a sense of possible purpose working itself out in history.

Never before had Adams been able to discern the working of law in history, which was the reason of his failure in teaching it, for chaos cannot be taught; but he thought he had a personal property by inheritance in this proof of sequence and intelligence in the affairs of man; and this personal triumph left him a little cold towards the other diplomatic results of the war. He knew that Porto Rico must be taken, but he would have been glad to escape the Philippines. He knew the West Indies well enough to be assured that, whatever the American people might think or say about it, they would sooner or later have to police those islands, not against Europe, but for Europe, and America too; and one felt no call to shoulder the load of archipelagoes in the antipodes when one was trying painfully to pluck up courage to face the labor of shouldering archipelagoes at home. The country decided otherwise, and one acquiesced readily enough. After all, friends had done the work, if not one's self, and he too serves a certain purpose who only stands and cheers.

In June, at the crisis of interest, the Camerons came over, and took the fine old house of Surrenden Dering in Kent which they made a sort of country house to the Embassy. There, on a hot July 4, 1898, to an expectant group under the shady trees, came the telegram announcing the destruction of the Spanish Armada, as it might have come to Queen Elizabeth in 1588; and there, later in the season, came the order summoning Hay to the State Department.

Hay had no wish to be Secretary of State. He much preferred to remain Ambassador, and his friends were quite as cold about it as he. The discussion on both sides was earnest, but the decided voice of the conclave was that, though if he were a mere office-seeker he might certainly decline promotion, if he were a member of the Government he could not. No serious statesman could accept a favor and refuse a service. For him, no doubt, the service, though hard, might bring some share of profit, but for the friends who gave this unselfish decision, all would prove loss. For one, Adams on that subject had become a little daft. No one in his experience had ever passed unscathed through that malarious marsh. In his fancy, office was poison; it killed--body and soul--physically and socially. Yet the poison he complained of was not ambition; his poison was that of the will--the distortion of sight--the warping of mind--the degradation of tissue--the coarsening of taste--the narrowing of sympathy to the emotions of a caged rat. Hay's only ambition was to escape annoyance, and no one knew better than he that, at sixty years of age, sensitive to physical strain, still more sensitive to brutality, vindictiveness, or betrayal, he took office at cost of life.

Neither he nor any of the Surrenden circle made pretence of gladness at the new dignity, for, with all his gaiety of manner and lightness of wit, he took dark views of himself, and his obedience to the President's order was the gloomiest acquiescence he had ever smiled. Hay shouldered his pack and started for home. Adams had no mind to lose his friend without a struggle, though he had never known such sort of struggle to avail; so, as soon as the Surrenden establishment broke up, on October 17, he prepared for return home, and on November 13, none too gladly, found himself again gazing into La Fayette Square.

He had made another false start and lost two years more of education. He had nothing to do with Hay's politics, nor did Hay care whether his friends agreed or disagreed. All they tried to save was the personal relation. Even there, Adams would have been beaten had he not been helped by Mrs. Hay, who saw the necessity of distraction, and led her husband into the habit of stopping every afternoon to take his friend off for an hour's walk, followed by a cup of tea with Mrs. Hay afterwards.

For the moment, therefore, the situation was saved, at least in outward appearance, and on March 22, Adams was able to sail with the Lodges for Europe and to pass April in Sicily and Rome.

Forty years had left little of the Palermo that Garibaldi had shown to the boy of 1860, but Sicily in all ages seems to have taught only catastrophe and violence. For a lesson in anarchy, without a shade of sequence, Sicily stands alone and defies evolution. Yet even Rome was not mute, and the church of Ara Coeli seemed more and more to draw all the threads of thought to a centre, for every new journey led back to its steps--Karnak, Delphi, Syracuse--all lying on the road to the Capitol. They carried camel-loads of moral; and New York sent most of all, for, in forty years, America had made so vast a stride to empire that the world of 1860 stood already on a distant horizon somewhere on the same plane with the republic of Brutus and Cato.

Nothing annoyed Americans more than to be told this simple and obvious--in no way unpleasant--truth; therefore one sat silent as ever on the Capitol; but, by way of completing the lesson, the Lodges added a pilgrimage to Assisi and an interview with St. Francis, whose solution of historical riddles seemed the most satisfactory--or sufficient--ever offered. The most bewildering effect on the old Assistant Professor of 1874 was the contrast between what he had taught then and what he found himself confusedly trying to learn five-and-twenty years afterwards. At Harvard College, weary of spirit in the wastes of Anglo-Saxon law, he had occasionally given way to outbursts of derision at shedding his life-blood for the sublime truths of Sac and Soc:--

HIC JACET
HOMUNCULUS SCRIPTOR
 DOCTOR BARBARICUS
   HENRICUS ADAMS
 ADAE FILIUS ET EVAE
   PRIMO EXPLICUIT
       SOCNAM

He meant as satire the claim that he had been first to explain the legal meaning of Sac and Soc; but the whole point of view had vanished in 1900. Not he, but Sir Henry Maine and Rudolph Sohm, were the parents or creators of Sac and Soc. Convinced that the clue of religion led to nothing, and that politics led to chaos, one had turned to the law, as one's scholars turned to the Law School, because one could see no other path to a profession.

The law had proved as futile as politics or religion, or any other single thread spun by the human spider. St. Francis expressed supreme contempt for them all, and solved the whole problem by rejecting it altogether. Adams returned to Paris with a broken and contrite spirit, prepared to admit that his life had no meaning, and conscious that in any case it no longer mattered. He passed a summer of solitude contrasting sadly with the last at Surrenden; but the solitude did what the society did not--it forced and drove him into the study of his ignorance in silence. Here at last he entered the practice of his final profession. By way of a summer school, he began a methodical survey--a triangulation--of the twelfth century. In the long summer days one found a sort of saturated green pleasure in the forests, and gray infinity of rest in the little twelfth-century churches that lined them, as unassuming as their own mosses, and as sure of their purpose as their round arches.

His solitude was broken in November by the chance arrival of John La Farge. The American mind--the Bostonian as well as the Southern or Western--likes to walk straight up to its object, and assert or deny something that it takes for a fact. The most disconcerting trait of John La Farge was his reversal of the process. His approach was quiet and indirect; he moved round an object, and never separated it from its surroundings; he prided himself on faithfulness to tradition and convention; he was never abrupt and abhorred dispute.

One was never quite sure of his whole meaning until too late to respond, for he had no difficulty in carrying different shades of contradiction in his mind. Even a contradiction was to him only a shade of difference, a complementary color, about which no intelligent artist would dispute. Constantly he repulsed argument: "Adams, you reason too much!" was one of his standing reproaches. He should have blamed Adams for being born in Boston. The mind resorts to reason for want of training, and Adams had never met a perfectly trained mind.

To La Farge, eccentricity meant convention; a mind really eccentric never betrayed it. True eccentricity was a tone--a shade--a nuance. One evening Humphreys Johnston asked him to meet Whistler at dinner. At that moment the Boer War was raging, and, as every one knows, on that subject Whistler raged worse than the Boers. For two hours he declaimed against England--witty, declamatory, extravagant, bitter, amusing, and noisy; but in substance what he said was not merely commonplace--it was true! Yet La Farge was silent, and this difference of expression was a difference of art. Whistler in his art carried the sense of nuance and tone far beyond any point reached by La Farge; but in talk he showed a willingness to seem eccentric where no real eccentricity, unless perhaps of temper, existed.

This vehemence, which Whistler never betrayed in his painting, La Farge seemed to lavish on his glass. Whatever its value, it led Adams back to the twelfth century and to Chartres, where La Farge not only felt at home, but felt a sort of ownership. In conversation La Farge's mind was opaline with infinite shades and refractions of light, and with color toned down to the finest gradations. In glass it was insubordinate; it was renaissance; it asserted his personal force with depth and vehemence of tone never before seen.

La Farge's health became more and more alarming, and Adams was glad to get him safely back to New York, January 15, 1900, while he himself went at once to Washington to find out what had become of Hay. Hay's troubles had begun, and were quite as great as he had foreseen; but all this worry on Hay's account fretted Adams not nearly so much as the Boer War did on his own. To Adams the war became almost a personal outrage. He had been taught from childhood, even in England, that his forbears and their associates in 1776 had settled, once for all, the liberties of the British free colonies, and he very strongly objected to being forced to sit down, a hundred and fifty years after John Adams had begun the task, to prove, by appeal to law and fact, that George Washington was not a felon, whatever might be the case with George III. For reasons still more personal, he declined peremptorily to entertain question of the felony of John Adams.

Trained early, in the stress of civil war, to hold his tongue, he would not bother Hay with theoretical objections which were every day fretting him in practical forms. Hay's chance lay in patience and good-temper till the luck should turn; but as political education the point seemed vital to Adams. Practical politics consists in ignoring facts, but education and politics are two different and often contradictory things.

Hay turned to McKinley, whose judgment of men was finer than common in Presidents. McKinley undertook to pool interests in a general trust into which every interest should be taken, more or less at its own valuation, and whose mass should, under his management, create efficiency. He achieved very remarkable results. How much they cost was another matter.

Himself a marvellous manager of men, McKinley found several manipulators to help him, one of whom was Hay; but unfortunately Hay's strength was weakest and his task hardest. At home, interests could be easily combined by simply paying their price; but abroad whatever helped on one side, hurt him on another. Hay thought England must be brought first into the combine; but at that time Germany, Russia, and France were all combining against England, and the Boer War helped them. For the moment Hay had no ally, abroad or at home, except Pauncefote, and Adams always maintained that Pauncefote alone pulled him through.

Yet the difficulty abroad was far less troublesome than the obstacles at home. The Senate had grown more and more unmanageable.

"A treaty of peace, in any normal state of things," said Hay, "ought to be ratified with unanimity in twenty-four hours. They wasted six weeks in wrangling over this one, and ratified it with one vote to spare. We have five or six matters now demanding settlement. I should have a majority in every case, but a malcontent third would certainly dish every one of them. So that the real duties of a Secretary of State seem to be three: to fight claims upon us by other States; to press more or less fraudulent claims of our own citizens upon other countries; to find offices for the friends of Senators when there are none. Is it worth while--for me--to keep up this useless labor?"

To Adams the spectacle was so familiar as to be humorous. The fathers had intended to neutralize the energy of government and had succeeded, but their machine was never meant to do the work of a twenty-million horse-power society in the twentieth century. As a matter of mechanics, so much work must be done; bad machinery merely added to friction.

Always unselfish, generous, easy, patient, and loyal, Hay had treated the world as something to be taken in block without pulling it to pieces to get rid of its defects; he liked it all: he laughed and accepted. Yet even the gayest of tempers succumbs at last to constant friction. The old friend was rapidly fading. The habit remained, but the easy intimacy, the careless gaiety, the casual humor, were sinking into the routine of office; the wit and humor shrank within the blank walls of politics, and the irritations multiplied. To a head of bureau, the result seemed ennobling.

Although, as education, this branch of study was older than the twelfth century, the task of bringing the two periods into a common relation was new. Ignorance required that the values of the twelfth and twentieth centuries should be correlated in some relation of movement that could be expressed in mathematics, nor did one care in the least that all the world said it could not be done, or that one knew not enough mathematics even to figure a formula beyond the schoolboy s = gt^2/2. If Kepler and Newton could take liberties with the sun and moon, an obscure person in a remote wilderness like La Fayette Square could take liberties with Congress, and venture to multiply half its attraction into the square of its time.

All his associates in history condemned such an attempt as futile and almost immoral. He looked about him in vain for a teacher. He had been much in the habit of turning to Langley, of the Smithsonian, whenever he wanted an outlet for his vast reservoirs of ignorance. Langley listened with outward patience to his disputatious questionings; but he too nourished a scientific passion for doubt, and sentimental attachment for its avowal. He generously let others doubt what he felt obliged to affirm; and early put into Adams's hands the "Concepts of Modern Science," a volume by Judge Stallo, which had been treated for a dozen years by the schools with a conspiracy of silence such as inevitably meets every revolutionary work that upsets the stock and machinery of instruction. Adams read and failed to understand; then he asked questions and failed to get answers.

Probably this was education. For him the details of science meant nothing: he wanted to know its mass. Kinetic atoms led only to motion; never to direction or progress. History had no use for multiplicity; it needed unity; it could study only motion, direction, attraction, relation. Everything must be made to move together; one must seek new worlds to measure; and so, like Rasselas, Adams set out once more, and found himself on May 12 settled in rooms at the very door of the Trocadero.

comment.original_text:
OF the year 1862 Henry Adams could never think without a shudder. The war alone did not greatly distress him. He was used to seeing people wade in blood, and he could plainly discern in history that man from the beginning had found his chief amusement in bloodshed. But the ferocious joy of destruction at its best requires that one should kill what one hates, and young Adams neither hated nor wanted to kill his friends the rebels, while he wanted nothing so much as to wipe England off the earth. Never could any good come from that besotted race! Every day the British Government deliberately crowded him one step further into the grave. The Trent Affair showed where Palmerston and Russell stood. The escape of the rebel cruisers from Liverpool was not, in a young man's eyes, the sign of hesitation, but the proof of their fixed intention to intervene. In private no political opponent in England, and few political friends, hesitated to say brutally of Lord John Russell that he lied. This was no great reproach, for, more or less, every statesman lied. The intensity of the private secretary's rage sprang from his belief that Russell's form of defence covered intent to kill. Not for an instant did the Legation draw a free breath. The suspense was hideous and unendurable.

The Minister, no doubt, endured it, but he had support and consideration. His son had nothing to think about but his friends, who were mostly dying under McClellan in the swamps about Richmond, or his enemies, who were exulting in Pall Mall. When the story of the second Bull Run appeared, he could bear it no longer. After a sleepless night, walking up and down his room without reflecting that his father was beneath him, he announced at breakfast his intention to go home into the army. His mother seemed to be less impressed by the announcement than by the walking over her head, which was so unlike her as to surprise her son. Mr. Adams took his son's defection as quietly as he took Bull Run, but his son never got the chance to go. The remonstrances of his brother Charles had much to do with delaying action. Henry also felt, of his own accord, that if he deserted his post in London and found the Capuan comforts he expected in Virginia, where he would have only bullets to wound him, he would never forgive himself. He would be leaving his father and mother alone to be devoured by the wild beasts of the British amphitheatre. This reflection might not have stopped him, but his father's suggestion was decisive. The Minister pointed out that it was too late for him to take part in the actual campaign, and that long before next spring they would all go home together.

The young man had copied too many affidavits about rebel cruisers to miss the point of this argument, so he sat down again to copy some more. Consul Dudley at Liverpool provided a continuous supply. The work was nothing. Not the work, but the play exhausted. The effort of facing a hostile society was bad enough, but that of facing friends was worse. After terrific disasters like the seven days before Richmond and the second Bull Run, friends needed support. A tone of bluff would have been fatal; nothing answers but candor. Yet private secretaries never feel candid, however much they feel the reverse, and therefore they must affect candor. If one shed tears, they must be shed on one's pillow. One must read one's Times every morning over one's muffin without reading aloud--"Another disastrous Federal Defeat"; and one might not even indulge in harmless profanity. Self-restraint among friends required much more effort than keeping a quiet face before enemies. Great men were the worst blunderers. One day the private secretary was standing with the crowd in the throne-room, and he smiled at hearing, behind his shoulder, one Cabinet Minister remark gaily to another: "So the Federals have got another licking!" The point of the remark was its truth. Even a private secretary had learned to betray no joy over the "lickings" of an enemy--in the enemy's presence.

London was altogether beside itself on one point. It created a nightmare of its own, and gave it the shape of Abraham Lincoln. Behind this it placed another demon, if possible more devilish, and called it Mr. Seward. Defence was useless; explanation was vain; one could only let the passion exhaust itself. One's best friends were as unreasonable as enemies. The last time Henry Adams saw Thackeray, before his sudden death at Christmas in 1863, was in entering the house of Sir Henry Holland for an evening reception. Thackeray was pulling on his coat downstairs, laughing because he had stumbled into the wrong house. Then his tone changed as he spoke of his--and Adams's--friend, Mrs. Frank Hampton, of South Carolina, whom he had loved as Sally Baxter and painted as Ethel Newcome. She had died of consumption at Columbia while her parents and sister were refused permission to pass through the lines to see her. In speaking of it, Thackeray's voice trembled and his eyes filled with tears. He never doubted that the Federals made a business of harrowing the tenderest feelings of women--particularly of women--in order to punish their opponents. On quite insufficient evidence he burst into violent reproach. At that moment Thackeray, and all London society with him, needed the nervous relief of expressing emotion; for if Mr. Lincoln was not what they said he--was what were they?

For like reason, the members of the Legation kept silence, even in private, under the boorish Scotch jibes of Carlyle. Demolition of one's idols is painful, and Carlyle had been an idol. Not merely the idols fell, but also the habit of faith. If Carlyle, too, was a fraud, what were his scholars and school?

Society as a rule was civil, but one's few friends in society were mere ornament. Henry Adams went his way peacefully enough. He went where he was asked; he was always courteously received; and he held his tongue.

For a thousand reasons, the best diplomatic house in London was Lord Palmerston's, while Lord John Russell's was one of the worst. The Queen herself, in her famous memorandum of August 12, 1850, gave her opinion of Palmerston in words that differed little from Lord John Russell's. Yet the diplomatic standard of trust seemed to be other than the parliamentarian. The worst liars were the candid. What diplomatists wanted to know was the motive that lay beyond the expression. In the case of Palmerston, they were unanimous in warning new colleagues that they might expect to be sacrificed by him to any momentary personal object. If he had an object to gain, he would go down to the House of Commons and betray or misrepresent a foreign Minister, without concern for his victim. No one got back on him with a blow equally mischievous--not even the Queen--for, as old Baron Brunnow described him: "C'est une peau de rhinocere!"

Diplomatists have no right to complain of mere lies, but they complain bitterly of traps. Palmerston was believed to lay traps. On the other hand, Lady Palmerston was believed to be good and loyal, and the diplomats and their wives took their troubles to her. Her evenings at home had great vogue. Lady Palmerston was no longer young or handsome. The people one met there were never smart and seldom young. They were largely diplomatic, and diplomats are commonly dull. Yet, beyond a doubt, Cambridge House was the best, and perhaps the only political house in London. Its success was due to Lady Palmerston, who never seemed to make an effort beyond a friendly recognition. The world never explains such riddles. The foreigners said only that Lady Palmerston was "sympathique."

The small fry of the Legations were tolerated there, and could at least stand in a corner and look at a bishop or even a duke. No one knew young Adams--not even the lackeys. On the last Saturday evening he ever attended, he gave his name as usual at the foot of the staircase. He was rather disturbed to hear it shouted up as "Mr. Handrew Hadams!" He tried to correct it, and the footman shouted more loudly: "Mr. Hanthony Hadams!" With some temper he repeated the correction, and was finally announced as "Mr. Halexander Hadams," and under this name made his bow for the last time to Lord Palmerston who certainly knew no better.

Far down the staircase one heard Lord Palmerston's laugh as he stood at the door receiving his guests. The laugh was singular, mechanical, wooden, and did not seem to disturb his features. "Ha! ... Ha! ... Ha!" Each was a slow, deliberate ejaculation, as though he meant to say: "Yes! ... Yes! ... Yes!" by way of assurance. It was a laugh of 1810 and the Congress of Vienna. One made the usual bow and received the usual glance of civility. Then one passed on to Lady Palmerston, who was always kind in manner but wasted no remarks.

By some process of personal affiliation, Minister Adams succeeded in persuading himself that he could trust Lord Russell more safely than Lord Palmerston. His son, being young and ill-balanced in temper, thought there was nothing to choose. Minister Adams had much to learn, although with him as well as with his son, the months of education began to count as aeons.

Just as Brunnow predicted, Lord Palmerston made his rush at last, as unexpected as always. It was late one afternoon in June, 1862. The private secretary had returned with the Minister from some social function, and he saw his father pick up a note from his desk and read it in silence. Then he said curtly: "Palmerston wants a quarrel!" Palmerston wanted a quarrel; he must not be gratified; he must be stopped. The matter of quarrel was General Butler's famous woman-order at New Orleans. The motive was the belief in President Lincoln's brutality that had taken such deep root in the British mind. The Minister took for granted that Palmerston meant to score a diplomatic point by producing this note in the House of Commons. If he did this at once, the Minister was lost.

The moment was nervous--as far as the private secretary knew, quite the most critical moment in the records of American diplomacy--but the story belongs to history, not to education. His father succeeded in muzzling Palmerston without a public scandal. That was not enough for a private secretary who liked going to Cambridge House, and was puzzled to reconcile contradictions. The correspondence was conducted feebly on Palmerston's side. He allowed the United States Minister to close it by a refusal to receive further communications from him except through Lord Russell. The step was excessively strong, for it broke off private relations as well as public, and cost even the private secretary his invitations to Cambridge House. Mr. Adams was never more cool. He could conceive no other way of protecting his Government than to force Lord Russell to interpose. He believed that Palmerston's submission and silence were due to Russell. Perhaps he was right; at the time, his son had no doubt of it, though afterwards he felt less sure. Palmerston wanted a quarrel; the motive seemed evident; yet when the quarrel was made, he backed out of it; for some reason it seemed that he did not want it--at least, not then. Incredible as it seemed, he behaved like a well-bred gentleman who felt himself in the wrong. Still, the private secretary would have felt his education in politics more complete had he ever finally made up his mind on one point. Was Palmerston more angry with General Butler, or more annoyed at himself, for committing what was in both cases an unpardonable betise?

The year 1862 was a dark spot in Henry Adams's life, and the education it gave was mostly one that he gladly forgot. As far as he was aware, he made no friends. Yet towards the close of the year he was flattered by an invitation from Monckton Milnes to Fryston. It was one of many acts of charity towards the young that gave Milnes immortality. Milnes made it his business to be kind. A dispirited, disheartened private secretary was exceedingly grateful, and never forgot the kindness. Milnes was never like anybody, and his country parties served his purpose of mixing strange elements. In the winter mists of Yorkshire, his singular guests had nothing to do but astonish each other, if anything could astonish such men. Of the five, Adams alone was tame; he alone added nothing to the wit or humor, except as a listener; but they needed a listener and he was useful. Milnes was the oldest, and perhaps the sanest. He had sought contact with everybody and everything that Europe could offer, and knew it all chiefly as humorous.

The second guest was a quiet, singularly agreeable gentleman of the literary class, whom Milnes called Stirling of Keir. Milnes gave the hint that Stirling was violent only on one point--hatred of Napoleon III. The third guest Adams had already met at Lady Palmerston's, carrying his arm in a sling. He was Lawrence Oliphant, just from Japan, where he had been wounded in the fanatics' attack on the British Legation.

The fourth was a boy, or had the look of one, though in fact he was a year older than Adams himself. He resembled in action a tropical bird, high-crested, long-beaked, quick-moving, with rapid utterance and screams of humor, quite unlike any English lark or nightingale. Milnes introduced him as Mr. Algernon Swinburne. Milnes lingered in Adams's room to add that Swinburne had written some poetry, not yet published, of really extraordinary merit. Adams only wondered what more Milnes would discover, and whether by chance he could discover merit in a private secretary. He was capable of it.

At dinner, conversation ran first to Oliphant, who told his dramatic story simply, until Milnes thought it time to bring Swinburne out. Then, at last, if never before, Adams acquired education. What he had sought so long, he found; but he was none the wiser; only the more astonished. In 1862 smoking was forbidden indoors. But Monckton Milnes was a licensed libertine, and he let his guests smoke in Adams's bedroom, since Adams was an American-German barbarian ignorant of manners. There, after dinner, all sat--or lay--till far into the night, listening to the rush of Swinburne's talk. In a long experience, before or after, no one ever approached it.

The others could not believe his incredible memory and knowledge of literature, classic, mediaeval, and modern. He could recite a play of Sophocles or a play of Shakespeare, forward or backward, from end to beginning; or Dante, or Villon, or Victor Hugo. Swinburne was millions of ages far from them, yet he united them by his humor even more than by his poetry.

Late at night, Stirling of Keir wanted to take with him to his chamber a copy of "Queen Rosamund," the only volume Swinburne had then published. Adams offered to light him down with his solitary bedroom candle. All the way, Stirling was ejaculating explosions of wonder. At the foot of the stairs he paused, and burst out: "He's a cross between the devil and the Duke of Argyll!"

To appreciate the full merit of this description, a judicious critic should have known both, and Henry Adams knew only one. But he understood that to a Scotchman the likeness meant something quite portentous, supernatural, and what the French call moyenageux. The idea that one has actually met a real genius dawns slowly on a Boston mind, but it made entry at last.

Then came the sad reaction, not from Swinburne, whose genius never was in doubt, but from the Boston mind, which in its uttermost flights was never moyenageux. To Swinburne, Adams could be no more than a worm. The quality of genius was an education almost ultimate, for one touched there the limits of the human mind on that side; but one could only receive; one had nothing to give--nothing even to offer.

Swinburne tested him then and there by one of his favorite tests--Victor Hugo. Adams tried to evade Swinburne's vehement insistence by parading an affection for Alfred de Musset. Swinburne would have none of it; de Musset was unequal; he did not sustain himself on the wing. Swinburne tried him again on Walter Savage Landor, and Adams's failure was equally gross. When forced to despair, he had to admit that both Hugo and Landor bored him. Nothing more was needed. One who could feel neither Hugo nor Landor was lost.

The sentence was just and Adams never appealed from it. He knew he was no companion for Swinburne. Only in France is the attitude of prayer possible; in England it became absurd. Even Monckton Milnes, who felt the splendors of Hugo and Landor, was almost as helpless as an American private secretary in personal contact with them. Ten years afterwards Adams met him at the Geneva Conference, fresh from Paris, bubbling with delight at a call he had made on Hugo.

"I was shown into a large room," Milnes said, "with women and men seated in chairs against the walls, and Hugo at one end throned. No one spoke. At last Hugo raised his voice solemnly, and uttered the words: 'Quant a moi, je crois en Dieu!' Silence followed. Then a woman responded as if in deep meditation: 'Chose sublime! un Dieu qui croit en Dieu!'"

With the best of will, one could not do this in London. Yet even a private secretary was not wholly wanting in instinct. As soon as he reached town he hurried to Pickering's for a copy of "Queen Rosamund." He would have offered Swinburne a solemn worship as Milnes's female offered Hugo, if it would have pleased the poet. Unfortunately it was worthless.

The three young men returned to London, and each went his own way. "The London season," Milnes used to say, "is a season for making acquaintances and losing friends." Adams sat next to Swinburne once more, at a dinner of the Authors' Fund over which Milnes presided. Swinburne was famous then, but no nearer, and they never met again. The only record of the visit may perhaps exist still in the registers of the St. James's Club. Immediately afterwards Milnes proposed Henry Adams for membership, with seconders a little singular for variety. On the whole, the list suggested that the private secretary was getting on.

comment.original_text:
On Moran's promotion to be Secretary, Mr. Seward inquired whether Minister Adams would like the place of Assistant Secretary for his son. It was the first--and last--office ever offered him, if indeed he could claim what was offered in fact to his father. To them both, the change seemed useless. Any young man could make some sort of Assistant Secretary; only one, just at that moment, could make an Assistant Son. His position was abnormal. In the Legation, as private secretary, he was liable to do Secretary's work. In society, when official, he was attached to the Minister; when unofficial, he was a young man without any position at all. The position was irregular; at that time many positions were irregular; yet it lent itself to a sort of irregular education that seemed to be the only sort of education the young man was ever to get.

Such as it was, few young men had more. The spring and summer of 1863 saw a great change in Secretary Seward's management of foreign affairs. He felt, at last, that his official representatives abroad needed support. In order to affect European opinion, the weight of American opinion had to be brought to bear personally, and had to be backed by the weight of American interests. Mr. Seward set vigorously to work and sent over every important American on whom he could lay his hands. All came to the Legation more or less intimately, and Henry Adams had a chance to see them all, bankers or bishops, who did their work quietly and well, though the work seemed wasted. The waste was only apparent; the work all told in the end, and meanwhile it helped education.

The most interesting of these was Thurlow Weed, who came to do what the private secretary himself had attempted two years before, with boyish ignorance of his own powers. Mr. Weed took charge of the press, and began, to the amused astonishment of the secretaries, by making what the Legation had learned to accept as the invariable mistake of every amateur diplomat; he wrote letters to the London Times. Thurlow Weed was a complete American education in himself. Before Mr. Weed went away, young Adams followed him about not only obediently--for obedience had long since become a blind instinct--but rather with sympathy and affection, much like a little dog.

The trait that astounded and confounded cynicism was his apparent unselfishness. The effect of power and publicity on all men is the aggravation of self, a sort of tumor that ends by killing the victim's sympathies; and Thurlow Weed was one of the exceptions; a rare immune. He grasped power, but not office. He had the instinct of empire: he gave, but he did not receive. Management was an instinct with Mr. Weed; an object to be pursued for its own sake, as one plays cards; but he appeared to play with men as though they were only cards; he seemed incapable of feeling himself one of them. Once, when he had told, with his usual humor, some stories of his political experience which were strong even for the Albany lobby, the private secretary made bold to ask him outright: "Then, Mr. Weed, do you think that no politician can be trusted?" Mr. Weed hesitated for a moment; then said in his mild manner: "I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so."

This lesson, at the time, translated itself to Adams in a moral sense, as though Mr. Weed had said: "Youth needs illusions!" As he grew older he rather thought that Mr. Weed looked on it as a question of how the game should be played. Young men most needed experience. Every card had a relative value. Principles had better be left aside; values were enough. Secretary Seward sent William M. Evarts to London as law counsel, and Henry began an acquaintance with Mr. Evarts that soon became intimate. Evarts was as individual as Weed was impersonal; he cared little for the game, and much for the stakes, but he played it in a large and liberal way, like Daniel Webster, "a great advocate employed in politics." Evarts was also an economist of morals, but with him the question was rather how much morality one could afford. "The world can absorb only doses of truth," he said; "too much would kill it." One sought education in order to adjust the dose.

The teachings of Weed and Evarts were practical, and the private secretary's life turned on their value. England's power of absorbing truth was small. Palmerston, Russell, and the society represented by the Times and Morning Post offered a study in education that sickened a young student with anxiety. He had begun--contrary to Mr. Weed's advice--by taking their bad faith for granted. Was he wrong? To settle this point became the main object of the diplomatic education so laboriously pursued, at a cost already stupendous, and promising to become ruinous. Life changed front, according as one thought one's self dealing with honest men or with rogues.

The recognition of belligerency, the management of the Declaration of Paris, the Trent Affair, all strengthened the belief that Lord Russell had started in May, 1861, with the assumption that the Confederacy was established, and was waiting only for the proper moment to interpose. No one in the Legation would have doubted it, except that Lord Russell obstinately denied the whole charge, and persisted in assuring Minister Adams of his honest and impartial neutrality. With the insolence of youth and zeal, Henry Adams jumped at once to the conclusion that Earl Russell--like other statesmen--lied; and, although the Minister thought differently, he had to act as though Russell were false. The most costly tutors in the world were provided for him at public expense--Lord Palmerston, Lord Russell, Mr. Gladstone, Lord Granville, and their associates, paid by the British Government; William H. Seward, Charles Francis Adams, William Maxwell Evarts, Thurlow Weed, and other considerable professors employed by the American Government; but there was only one student to profit by this immense staff of teachers. The private secretary alone sought education.

The stages of demonstration began in June, 1862, by the remonstrances of the Minister against the escape of "No. 290," which was imminent. Lord Russell declined to act on the evidence. New evidence was sent in every few days, and with it, on July 24, was included Collier's legal opinion: "It appears difficult to make out a stronger case of infringement of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which, if not enforced on this occasion, is little better than a dead letter." Such language implied almost a charge of collusion with the rebel agents--an intent to aid the Confederacy. In spite of the warning, Earl Russell let the ship, four days afterwards, escape.

Lord Russell undertook to disprove the inference that no statesman could be trusted. This new actor, as every one knows, was William Ewart Gladstone, then Chancellor of the Exchequer. If one man lived who could be certainly counted as sane by overwhelming interest, it was the man who had in charge the finances of England. From him, if from no one else, the poor student could safely learn.

Here is what he learned! Palmerston notified Gladstone, September 24, of the proposed intervention. Gladstone replied the next day that he desired the proceedings to be prompt, because of "the rapid progress of the Southern arms" and "the risk of violent impatience in the cotton-towns of Lancashire." The "truth" was not known for thirty years, but when published, seemed to be the reverse of Earl Russell's statement. Minister Adams bluntly told Russell that while he was "willing to acquit" Gladstone of "any deliberate intention to bring on the worst effects," Gladstone was doing it quite as certainly as if he had one. Russell replied, as guardedly as possible, that Lord Palmerston and others regretted the speech, and that it was still their intention "to adhere to the rule of perfect neutrality in the struggle, and to let it come to its natural end without the smallest interference, direct or otherwise." Minister Adams never knew more. He retained his belief that Russell could be trusted, but that Palmerston could not.

>
> Nov. 13. ... Palmerston gave to Russell's proposal a feeble and half-hearted support.

One would have done better to draw no conclusions at all. One's diplomatic education was a long mistake.

Palmerston hesitated; Russell insisted; Granville protested. On October 23, Russell assured Adams that no change in policy was now proposed. On the same day he had proposed it, and was voted down. Instantly Napoleon III appeared as the ally of Russell and Gladstone. The only resolute, vehement, conscientious champion of Russell, Napoleon, and Jefferson Davis was Gladstone.

Habitually Russell said one thing and did another. The young man did not complain of the falsehoods; on the contrary, he was vain of his own insight in detecting them; but he was wholly upset by the idea that Russell should think himself true. Russell ardently asserted that he had no objects, and that though he might be weak he was above all else honest. Education stopped there. No one, either in or out of England, ever offered a rational explanation of Earl Russell.

Palmerston was simple--so simple as to mislead the student altogether--but scarcely more consistent. The world thought him positive, decided, reckless; the record proved him to be cautious, careful, vacillating. He tried to check Russell. He scolded Gladstone. He discouraged Napoleon. Palmerston told no falsehoods; made no professions; concealed no opinions; was detected in no double-dealing. My offence was indeed only a mistake, but one of incredible grossness.... It illustrates vividly that incapacity which my mind so long retained, and perhaps still exhibits, an incapacity of viewing subjects all round....

Long and patiently--more than patiently--sympathetically, did the private secretary, forty years afterwards, read and re-read and reflect upon this confession. His whole theory of conspiracy--of policy--of logic and connection in the affairs of man, resolved itself into "incredible grossness." He felt no rancor, for he had won the game; he forgave, since he must admit, the "incapacity of viewing subjects all round" which had so nearly cost him life and fortune. Granting that Gladstone was party to no conspiracy; granting what the English themselves seemed at last to conclude--that Gladstone was not quite sane; that Russell was verging on senility; and that Palmerston had lost his nerve--what sort of education should have been the result of it?

Politics cannot stop to study psychology. Its methods are rough; its judgments rougher still. All this knowledge would not have affected either the Minister or his son in 1862. The Minister would still have found his interest in thinking Russell friendly and Palmerston hostile. The problem would have been the same; the answer equally obscure. Every student would, like the private secretary, answer for himself alone.

All came to the Legation more or less intimately, and Henry Adams had a chance to see them all, bankers or bishops, who did their work quietly and well, though the work seemed wasted. The waste was only apparent; the work all told in the end, and meanwhile it helped education.

The most interesting of these was Thurlow Weed, who came to do what the private secretary himself had attempted two years before, with boyish ignorance of his own powers.
